The 3:2 mean-motion resonance, particularly in systems with nearly circular orbits, is relatively easy to verify. However, demonstrating the resonance in systems with eccentric orbits is more complex and often requires greater differences in period ratios. Recent observations of the planetary system surrounding K2-138 have provided new data, including period changes for all five confirmed planets in the 1:2:4 resonance chain. Since the changes in the inner two planets' periods still indicate that the system needs further characterization to definitively prove it is in the 1:2:4 resonance, our analysis also focuses on K2-138, which contains planets near the 3:2 resonance with additional planets in the long-term mean motion average. Utilizing MCMC sampling as a novel technique, we determine a suitable period ratio goal of 0.013 for the third planet to be at resonance. Similar period ratio limits for the final two planets in the chain indicate they are likely out of the 1:2:4 resonance. The most effective method to verify resonances in systems like K2-138 includes analyzing stacking variations in the timescales of the oscillations over the course of the observations, which is particularly true for this specific planetary system. In wide-field X-ray astronomy, achieving an optimal balance between achieving the widest possible field of view and the highest possible angular resolution is a constant challenge. Historically, achieving an extended field of view necessarily meant sacrificing resolution, but the growing demand for comprehensive X-ray surveys has driven development of new optical systems designed to mitigate this trade-off. Our paper delves into the underlying design choices, analyzing the mechanical and optical complexities involved in designing these experiments. We begin by examining the fundamental trade-off between field of view and angular resolution, and then investigate how different optical design approaches can influence system-scale experiments. We consider the implications of using different types of X-ray lenses on an experiment's field of view and image quality. Our analysis reveals that, despite initial impressions, X-ray focal plane arrays do not universally enhance wide-field optical designs. In fact, these arrays tend to degrade the quality of point-source images, and may even reduce the effectiveness of detecting compact sources within their own radiation tails. To achieve impressive wide-field angular resolution, additional optical components are required, involving complex systems that can introduce substantial losses in the field of view and image intensity. The generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system (GNE(n)) is a polynomial Hamiltonian system, first mentioned by Levi et al. in 2006. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the symmetries and conservation laws for GNE(n) in any dimension $n$. It's discovered that the point symmetries of GNE(n) form a Lie algebra and that certain combinations of these symmetries constitute a soliton equation. Specifically, the combinations of two specific symmetries constitute the KdV equation, while the combination of three constitutes the Savvidis equation. Additionally, by using the Jacobi-Morawetz energy, two conservation laws for GNE(n) are identified. Notably, these combinations of symmetries are unique to GNE(n) and do not exist for its higher-dimensional counterpart, which was investigated by Yurinsky in 2015. This study further verifies a conjecture made by Levi et al. by proving the existence of a conservation law for a specific subset of polynomial Hamiltonian systems. This proof highlights the complexity of the problem in lower dimensions, such as $n=2$, and how the properties of conservation laws in these cases can be unpredictable. Lastly, this paper explores the relationship between the symmetries and a specific property of the generalized $2$-dimensional Ermakov system (GNE(2)). It's discovered that two specific symmetries are responsible for the robust conservation law of GNE(2), which is unique to GNE(2) and exists in no other polynomial Hamiltonian systems of higher dimensions. This study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the properties of Ermakov systems and their applications in physics and mathematics. Specifically, it explores the implications of the robust conservation law of GNE(2) on the properties of Lagrangian systems and the possibility of using these systems to model interacting particles. Moreover, this paper identifies a specific subset of conservative Lagrangian systems, which may be useful in modeling phenomena in physics and mathematics. Ultimately, this paper provides valuable insights into the behavior of physical systems and their applications in mathematics and physics. The Transit Feed Specification (TFS) enables unified data exchange between transit providers and feed processors by offering a range of coded feed types. Although TFS supports numerous coded feed types for various purposes like scheduling and stop data, there's a notable absence of feed types for routes, stops, and information accessibility in specific areas. To address this gap, researchers proposed adopting Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) for processing geospatial data and designing novel TFS feed types. For instance, an RNN-based feed type was developed to share route information with drivers, and another one was designed to update passengers on 365/367 days before a federal holiday. Furthermore, TFS feed specifications can be combined to generate more targeted and feature-rich feeds. To facilitate adoption without requiring network infrastructure, proposed feeds specification is available through a universal HTTPS URL, analogous to Google's auto-updating XML feed. Examples of unobtainable TFS feeds, along with their specified TFS feed types, are provided in the paper. While RNN technology is not yet applicable in production TFS feeds, the feasibility of using RNNs in processing geospatial data for TFS feeds is demonstrated. The integration of RNNs and TFS has the potential to expand the scope and versatility of transit data management and exchange. An associated GitHub project ('tfs-rnn') facilitates access to the presented TFS feeds specification and RNN-related materials. The project includes multiple branch RNN models, each corresponding to a distinct TFS feed type. Currently implemented RNN models include feed types for routes, stops within a radius of a given location, and areas with bounded stops. Furthermore, the project provides basic Jupyter Notebook code for RNN models, as well as a TFS feed generator, both designed for simplicity and ease of use. Given that RNN technology is not yet used in production, the project is initially accessible through a username and password authentication (for the 'tfs-rnn-admin' user), and the RNN-generated TFS feeds are not yet incorporated into feeding systems. To initiate the adoption of RNN technology, interested parties are invited to provide detailed route geometry data, schedule for scheduled routes, and high-quality geospatial stop data for dynamic updates. Once adopted, the presented RNN-based TFS feeds specification is intended to introduce new possibilities in the exchange of rich, informative transit data. This study shows that these persistent symmetries are associated with a 'Goldstone mode', which exhibits slow movement near low-energy levels, both in space and time. This finding is similar to the 'Goldstone theorem' previously established for static non-invertible symmetries. As an example, we examine the 'charge sliding' symmetry in 2D fractional topological insulators and illustrate how the theorem can be applied to this specific case. Our research also expands the existing framework of parity-odd generalized symmetries, parities, and polarities to include time-transposition, addressing the unique characteristics of time-reversal symmetry in fractional topological insulators. Moreover, we demonstrate that time-transposition parities emerge naturally from the action of time-reversal symmetry in systems described by 2D time-dependent Hamiltonians, even though time-reversal itself does not have a non-invertible representation. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings on the established theories of 2D fractional topological insulators. Our study delves into the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering across modal interactions within photonic lattice fibers containing solid core hosts made of materials like silicon and germanium, where the scattered photons typically reside in air-guiding photonic bandgap waveguides. We demonstrate both theoretically and experimentally that such modal interconnections give rise to a range of mechanical resonances with discrete eigenfrequencies, whose distances directly relate to the structure's geometric parameters. This mechanism is found to produce mechanical resonances about an order of magnitude greater than those in photonic crystal fibers with microstructured cores, while the conversion efficiency remains comparable. This unique property may be exploited to develop mechanical systems with spectral bottlenecks, as well as efficient two-photon exchange mechanisms between optical and acoustic domains. Moreover, we discuss how the structure of the solid core host material affects the characteristics of the confined phononic crystal, influencing the propagation of optical and acoustic waves. This investigation lays a crucial foundation for developing advanced mechanical systems with solid core photonic lattice fibers and identifying a range of applications in fields like nonlinear frequency conversion and quantum nanomechanics. To support and guide future research, comprehensive data and models are presented, including experimental results, theoretical calculations, and characterization maps of the mechanical resonances, the geometry of the solid core host, and the predicted phase matching conditions. This comprehensive resource is expected to facilitate similar investigations and assessments within the community. Furthermore, our experimental findings incorporate high-resolution spectroscopy techniques combined with precision measurements that involve tuning the optical frequency to minimize the backscatter efficiency. We successfully observed numerous mechanical resonances, accurately measured their frequencies, and mapped their relative strengths, ultimately demonstrating a versatile approach for detecting various intermodal Brillouin resonances. This study provides the first comprehensive analysis of forward Brillouin scattering in solid core photonic fiber systems through experimental and theoretical means, yielding crucial insights into mechanical resonance characteristics. It presents novel applications in mechanical tuning, optical modulation, and efficient nonlinear interactions. Importantly, our findings show that mechanical resonances with small optical mode imbalances are either very weak or undetectable. Consequently, two key scenarios remain feasible: either the optical tone is pinned to a specific mode, or the optical mode is unconfined and not pinned. Furthermore, our results indicate that mechanical tuning capabilities may be implemented; however, our ability to observe the reverse process is significantly limited due to the small optical mode imbalances. Conversely, our study reveals that mechanical resonance coupling is not necessary for detecting reverse Brillouin scattering through experimentally measured phase matching

Two key challenges in managing data across diverse applications and tasks are dataset selection and budget allocation.  The Knapsack problem for set-union datasets quantifies these challenges by optimizing a quantity (e.g., accuracy or loss) given constrained resources and a choice of sets.  We introduce the Knapsack problem as an instance of the recently defined set-union model, and the task is reduced to extracting a subset of desirable items from a chosen set.  We introduce the Budgeted Maximum Coverage problem, a related task of maximizing coverage given a limited budget and choosing elements from a set.  We develop a new search algorithm, called SubSet-Genie, and its variant, SubSet-Genie-Prod, for efficiently solving both the Knapsack and Budgeted Maximum Coverage problems.  We improve existing approaches by combining probabilistic techniques for efficient exploration and productive strategies for focusing search within promising subspaces.  We conduct extensive experiments using real-world image datasets and demonstrate that our algorithm, SubSet-Genie-Prod, outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions by a substantial margin, and its computational complexity is comparable or better in many cases.  We also show its applicability in multiple-instance learning settings where relation-based budgets are applied.  We believe that our work contributes to future research by providing a comprehensive understanding of the computational complexities associated with various task reductions.  The proposed algorithm and associated code are available for research purposes at https://github.com/harshgupta92/SumModel.  We apply our algorithm to successfully solve the Maximum Coverage problem and achieve state-of-the-art results in multi-label image classification tasks, and our findings are published in a paper at the IJCAI 2020.  We also obtain excellent results in winner-takes-all multi-label classification tasks and outperform existing solutions in single-instance learning settings as shown in a related study published at the CVPR 2021.  The results are further improved in a related study published at the CVPR 2021.  The related studies can be found at https://www.harshgupta92.com/pubs.html.  The proposed algorithm is also successfully applied in multi-label image classification tasks in a related study published at the CVPR 2021 as can be found at https://www.harshgupta92.com/pubs.html.  The proposed algorithm in the paper is also successfully extended in a related study published at the CVPR 2021 as can be found at https://www.harshgupt

This study customizes churn forecasting models to address the specific challenges of predicting customer churn in the online gambling industry, where a single significant event, such as winning, can instantly transform a customer into an inactive or a high-value customer. The model is tailored to accommodate the rare categorization of customers in the target domain - specifically, non-churner, churner, or delayed churner. The later is denoted as "delayed churner." The central aim is to identify customers who will stop betting within a specified timeframe. The research is based on an extensive dataset comprising 460 million real-time user records and showcases an average precision of 95% across various timeframes for predicting churner, delayed churner, and non-churner classifications using predictive models, such as FastText and RingLSTM, trained on streaming data featuring advanced features and designs. The model's effectiveness is measured by accuracy metrics, including F1-score and Hamming loss. The research highlights effective predictive models and key features essential for predicting customer churn in online gambling platforms. The model is further enhanced by incorporating dynamics in forecasting and evaluating predictions on streaming data with robust algorithms and metrics. The research demonstrates that robust algorithms like RingLSTM and streaming data remedies like Weighted Averaging and Hamming Loss can significantly contribute to predicting customer churn in online gambling. The model's key findings emphasize the value of constant and variable models in forecasting and the need to adjust the timing and accuracy of predictions accordingly. The research ultimately reveals that by combining insights from the three categories of customers, i.e. non-churner, churner, and delayed churner, we can develop a more effective model in forecasting and achieve better outcomes. The model's key insights show that delayed churners have more similarity with non-churner and churner, and non-churner has the least similarity with the two, while the model fails to accurately forecast delayed churner. The model's key insights also show that model's timing and accuracy are crucial factors in forecasting and should be considered and designed accordingly. The model's key insights further indicate that online gambling companies can reduce false positives by stopping forecasting early when a sufficient number of churning customers have been found, which helps reduce unnecessary costs and improve efficiency. The model's key insights also suggest that by incorporating delayed churner into forecasting, the model can achieve better outcomes and improve forecasting accuracy. The model's key insights provide valuable suggestions for improving forecasting in practice and can guide the development of future models in practice. The verification problem for quantum computations involves assessing whether a given quantum circuit produces the correct output for a specific input, using measurements in a finite number of runs. We've developed an efficient method to verify quantum circuits, especially those with Pauli-based gates and a single qubit depth of L, that runs in linear time complexity. This method works by analyzing the quantum circuit as a combination of L levels, creating a corresponding flow network, and applying Kerovski's theorem to verify the circuit's output in O(n^2 L) time. This method also runs in linear time when using quantum circuits with reversible gates, despite a higher qubit count. Furthermore, we've extended this method to verify quantum circuits with noisy conditions, allowing for the assessment of robustness against noise using Nesterov's inequality. We've confirmed our results with concrete runtime examples, showcasing superior performance in comparison to existing methods. This research was supported in part by a grant from the NSF. We've also utilized the associated verification tools, available at https://vivisector.github.io/VerQuant/verification.html. This method boasts a wide applicability, encompassing various types of quantum circuits, and can be leveraged in multiple fields, such as validation, testing, and fairness assessment for quantum-based applications. We've also demonstrated the effectiveness of noise assessment in quantum state preparation. Blind, low-vision, and print-impaired individuals still struggle with accessing standard document formats like PDF. A major obstacle is navigating these documents due to lack of accessibility guidelines and accessible navigation tools. Given existing document formats' limited potential for reform, implementing a universal set of accessibility guidelines becomes increasingly crucial. One such proposal, the Document Navigability Standard, seeks to address this issue by introducing a set of guidelines that enable users to navigate documents through audio cues. Our experiment tested the DN standard with actual documents, revealing that users can indeed navigate complex PDFs with relative ease. One method involved layering audio and visual cues, while another involved splitting long documents into audio-friendly sections. Our analysis of the data extracted from the experiment allowed us to assess the usability of the Document Navigability standard and pinpoint areas for further improvement. Our experiment not only evaluates the practicality of the DN standard but also identifies key requirements for creating navigable documents, including audio visualizations, audio navigation, table navigation, and segment splitting. Our discovery indicates that most PDFs can be made accessible through the application of the DN standard with minimal modification. Our proposed Document Navigability standard provides a foundational framework for creating accessible navigation tools, emphasizing the importance of system design in creating such tools. Our work seeks to inform future research and standardization efforts in creating accessible navigation systems, drawing from our participants' valuable feedback. Our experiment demonstrates that a well-designed document accessibility framework can have a significant impact on the lives of print-impaired individuals. Our work is particularly relevant due to the relative lack of research on creating accessible navigation systems, with most existing studies primary goals centered around specific technical areas rather than system design. Our experiment is part of a larger project aimed at improving accessibility through user-centered design approaches. Among these, 23 galaxies were found to have a prominent stellar disk when compared to their central compact sources that contain massive black holes. In contrast, 14 galaxies had a compact nuclear source that matches or surpasses the size of their surrounding disks. We closely examined the relationship between the size of these galaxies and their optical and infrared brightness using a dynamic model for their growth. It appears that the largest infrared brightness is linked to an increase in spiral arms and disk extent. Furthermore, it has been discovered that a significant portion of near-infrared excess emission in galaxies with extended disks comes from a significant distance away from their central point, rather than just nearby, while in galaxies with a compact nucleus, the near-infrared excess is mainly produced in a small area surrounding the central black hole. In both types of galaxies, the near-infrared and ultraviolet emissions are closely linked. We propose that the extended star formation that occurs in the disk of these galaxies is triggered by the outflow of mass caused by the central black hole, as this is the only explanation that can account for the diverse range of observed characteristics. In galaxies with a compact nucleus, it seems that the outflow of mass is limited to a very small area around the central black hole. In order for these galaxies to form massive, extended star-forming regions that resemble super star clusters, a significant shock event or other disturbances are required. The investigation of blocked disks in a channel has evident practical implications, including the navigation of large cargo ships and sailboarding across rivers with mechanical barriers. Previously, the critical aspect of determining sequences of non-overlapping disks has been studied extensively. In contrast, this research explores weighted disks, where each disk may have a specific weight, while maintaining the primary criterion of non-overlapping disks. A recursive function is introduced to facilitate identification of applicable sequences of blocked disks. Furthermore, the introduced concepts are illustrated through various examples. In addition, the introduced concepts are shown to be applicable in a diverse range of channel scenarios, including channels with an odd number of banks and those restricted in width. A comprehensive list of references is provided at the conclusion of this research. In conclusion, the introduced concepts present a novel method of analyzing and understanding sequences of blocked disks with weights. A method of generating applicable sequences of blocked disks via their weights is proposed. In addition, the introduced concepts are shown to have a connection to the concept of Fibonacci numbers. The diverse ENSO types and their impacts on precipitation around the world need to be better understood.  Research has shown that El Ni\~n events come in two main flavors - Central Pacific (EP) and Eastern Pacific (LP), which are associated with different climate behaviors.  By analyzing precipitation data from over 7,000 stations, this study uncovered how the two types of ENSO impacts variation in precipitation across different latitudes and times of year.  It was found that EP events tend to weaken precipitation in some areas that experience increased precipitation during El Ni\~n events, such as Hawaii, while LP events however, have a smaller occurrence rate in comparison to EP events.  Consequently, EP events were more frequently linked to very low precipitation, especially in some areas that experience increased precipitation during LP events.  This study documented the occurrence of substantial drought in areas such as western South America, which is more frequently linked to EP events.  Conversely, regions that normally experience high precipitation during LP events, such as the central USA, were instead associated with high precipitation during EP events.  This study revealed the varying impact of the two types of ENSO flavors and their distinct climate behaviors.  It was found that EP events have a more pronounced impact on high precipitation in regions like Japan and Indonesia, while LP events have a more significant impact on high precipitation in areas such as Mexico.  Researchers in this study pointed out the need for a better distinction between the two types of ENSO flavors in precipitation forecasting.  They for instance noticed that the notorious LP-induced rainfall disaster in Trinidad and Tobago tends to be over-predicted if EP-flavored rather than LP-flavored precipitation forecasts are used. Since non-affine behavior is difficult to observe in typical 2D images, we employ advanced optical techniques to study this phenomenon in lab-made and natural fractures, revealing a complex interplay between friction and friction reduction mechanisms. This investigation sheds light on the uncharted realm of dry fracturing and offers insights for modeling non-affine growth. The proposed methodology is versatile and can be applied to other complex physical processes. The observed patterns also imply that certain natural fractures may have originated from the actions of micro-organisms. The study concludes by exploring the broader implications of non-affine growth and the potential applications of optical tools in geology and materials science. The set of 66 molecular dimers in the S66 dataset has been used to study the influence of weak electric fields on non-covalent interactions.  Computational results for dipole moments, free energies, and interface charges were obtained through quantum mechanical and classical models, including path-integral simulations.  It was found that weak electric fields can cause large dipole moments to decrease, and experiments show that these quantum corrections are critical in understanding this phenomenon.  Furthermore, research has shown that polarizable models fail to capture the full extent of electrostatic effects between molecular pairs in response to an electric field, stressing the need for accurate quantum descriptions in chemical modeling.  Two-dimensional correlation plots were also analyzed to study the relationship between energy, dipole moment, and interface charge in the presence of an electric field, revealing distinct characteristics between closed and open shells, and leading to the development of a new parameter.  It was observed that low-frequency oscillations in dipole moment and interface charge are coupled and correlated with changes in energy, while high-frequency components show less correlation with these variations.  A new parameter, known as $\gamma_0$, was introduced to describe the synchrony of oscillations and showed strong correlation with electrostatic effects between molecular pairs in the presence of an electric field.  Additionally, research has demonstrated that these electrostatic effects are largely determined by low-frequency components and traditional models fail to capture the complexity of these high-frequency contributions.  A comprehensive list of computational and experimental results for dipole moment, free energy, and interface charge in the presence of electric fields is provided in the supplementary material.  It was found that experimental results for dipole moment match the sign monomer orientation scenario much better than the polar orientation.  Conversely, geometric modeling along with implicit solvent approach failed to reproduce the correct electrostatic effects observed through path-integral simulations.  Furthermore, research has shown that implicit solvent models overestimate interactions involving dimers with large dipole moments in the presence of electric fields.  Analyzing results from various functional main-group dimers showed that implicit solvent models overestimate electrostatic effects in polar dimers but underestimate electrostatic effects in non-polar dimers.  Frequency-dependent permittivity of vacuum obtained from perturbation theory at the level of second-order perturbation also failed to match the experimental results for dimers containing hydrogen-bonding capabilities. The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly improved industrial productivity and competitiveness through smart manufacturing and factory automation technologies, enabling highly controllable and predictable processes. Despite this, industrial scheduling systems still struggle to account for unpredictable processes and often rely on simplified statistical models or real-time data, risk overlooking crucial factors and resulting in suboptimal solutions. To address these limitations, we introduce an advanced probabilistic model for modelling uncertainty, enabling more accurate depiction and utilization in industrial scheduling systems. An integrated solver has been developed to optimize industrial schedules while taking various types of uncertainty into account, and we demonstrate its effectiveness using a real-world example from the Machine Shop problem. Compared to existing approaches, our results reveal a high degree of precision, showcasing up to a 5% improvement in efficiency. This research aims to contribute valuable industry insights and theoretical knowledge to solving similar challenges in industrial settings. By leveraging such solutions, manufacturers can more effectively tackle uncertainty in smart industrial applications and achieve optimized productivity. Cyber-Physical Systems require robust resilience properties to withstand disruptions in their physical components, as dictated by government mandates and as a critical consideration for system design. Resilience is particularly hard to define, letting alone precisely design, due to its flexibility in interpretation. To tackle this issue, a recent research approach relies on temporal logic, leveraging a Timed Logic-based Framework to outline and appraise Cyber-Physical Systems' resilience. A key concept within this approach involves Reaching States, which embody the system's resiliency goal after encountering Adversarial Affected Events. To validate the proposed method, a case study is presented on a CP system used for analyzing data in air quality monitoring. This study demonstrates the practical application of the approach in assessing CP systems resilience. To support future applications, the researchers intend to further develop the method, focusing on evaluating the likelihood and impact of potential disruptions, and the effectiveness of different mitigation strategies. A software tool is also being developed to facilitate design and analysis in the design lifecycle of CP systems. A forthcoming extension will incorporate Universal Temporal Logic, allowing the approach to address multiple resiliency goals in complex Multi-Agent systems such as those characterizing Smart Grids. Overall, the proposed method aims to bring resiliency design into the realm of formal design methodology, complementing the existing Cyber-Physical Systems engineering process. A major benefit of this approach is its potential to systematize a main aspect of CP systems design, which is currently largely unexplored due to the existing state-of-the-art limitations. Research goals include further developing the design method, integrating the approach into a design automation framework, and supporting the double lifecycle of CP systems, from conceptualization to CP software development. We explore various techniques for approximating the gradient of a real-valued function, $u$, which satisfies a specified nonlinear diffusion equation on a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold $M$. In this scenario, $u$ is deemed nonconstant. We establish different types of error lemmas with specific rates, which depend on the diffusion function $f$, introduced in a previous study (2018), and apply established Sobolev and Gaussian type inequalities in a recent paper (2020). These error lemmas, which differ based on the sign of $u$, leverage the manifold setting to obtain refined quantitative results. These are akin to those established in recent studies by Agostinachev, Kogut, and Vogeluchi, yet take into account the Riemannian manifold structure of the underlying space. We apply the obtained error lemmas to demonstrate global $C^{1, \gamma}$-estimates for the solution $u$ of the nonlinear diffusion equation. Furthermore, in the case of a strictly parabolic diffusion, these, in conjunction with the integration by parts technique and a recent lemma introduced by Agostinachev, Kogut, and Vogeluchi, enable the derivation of the global $C^{2, \gamma}$-estimates. We ultimately apply the obtained estimates to establish the solvability of Dirichlet problems for nonlinear diffusion equations on bounded domains with Dirichlet conditions. This work represents an expansion of the methods used in a study by Agostinachev and Kogut, which primarily focused on the Euclidean space setting. The primary step in our proof involves the characterization of the boundary in a transformed space and the application of the Ekeland-Maz'ya variational technique. We demonstrate the solvability of Dirichlet problems with singular diffusion and non-singular diffusion functions. In the case of singular diffusion, we impose the condition of subquadratic growth on the diffusion function $f$, while in the case of non-singular diffusion, we require subexponential growth. The obtained results encompass a broad range of diffusion functions, which may be identically zero or display spatial dependence, in addition to various types of growth conditions for the diffusion function $f$. This presents an expansion of the existing methods, which were primarily limited to zero order mean convex diffusion functions in the context of the Euclidean space setting. Two studies examining the properties of faint radio sources present an opportunity 
to analyze how these characteristics change with the size of the sources. 
Initial research involved data from the Very Large Array catalog containing sources 
up to 200 $\mu Jy$ with small angular diameters, while a second analysis used sources 
from the LOFAR-LS source survey with a broader range of angular sizes and source 
fluxes. By stacking sources according to their angular sizes, these studies were able 
to gain insights into how these sources relate to galaxy environments and the larger 
universe. Through cross-correlation of sources in these two studies, scientists were 
able to link low-frequency properties to high-frequency properties, leading to new 
discoveries about these enigmatic sources. Specifically, sources that appear more 
extended at low frequencies show an increased correlation with dark matter, 
notably through their relationship with galaxy cluster temperatures. This correlation 
holds significance in that it explains some of the variations in source density 
observed across different redshifts, a property known as "radio density gap". 
Moreover, sources with larger angular sizes also display a higher level of 
non-uniformity, which in turn is linked with properties of host galaxies, including 
their stellar mass and blue luminosity. This increased non-uniformity is found to 
diminish with the size of the sources, showing that smaller sources are more 
uniformly distributed. 
Key findings from these studies include the identification of two distinct types of 
compact radio sources. Sources near a specific kiloparsec scale are more 
asymmetrically distributed on the plane and show higher levels of stochasticity 
in their appearance. Additionally, sources within a certain range of 200-500 
kiloparsecs show minimal signs of stochasticity but exhibit marked dependencies 
on the characteristics of their host galaxies. 
It has also been observed that these sources primarily reside within a specific 
distance of 1.5 times the great distance wave, an observed phenomenon attributed to 
the ASPECT effect - a phenomenon where certain types of intergalactic medium 
interfer with and distort radiation from distant sources while exhibiting wave 
like patterns of density. 
Correlations between certain galaxy properties (including color, mass, blue and 
total luminosity) and sources found within specific (mass weighted) ranges also 
emerged through these research findings.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a type of mathematical model that describes a probabilistic process consisting of visible and hidden states. In the visible states, actions are taken that release observable information. HMMs are used in numerous fields, including speech recognition and DNA sequence analysis. HMMs can be conceptually extended in several directions, including combining probabilistic steps and incorporating self-referential states. This work presents a unified description of HMMs using a concept called information monads, effectively capturing the inherent flow of information present in these models. Additionally, we outline the general principles for adapting this concept to various probabilistic models. In addition to providing a clear, abstract definition of HMMs, this work offers an opportunity to explore more advanced mathematical structures, including monads and dualities in mathematics. A detailed mathematical examination of HMMs offers insights into the fundamental nature of probabilistic processes with hidden components. Moreover, defining HMMs in a abstract, top-down manner allows for a deeper understanding of what it means for a model to be hidden. This approach to defining HMMs also provides a framework for incorporating additional, quantitative aspects of information flow into the description, even if those details are not yet fully developed in mathematics. Finally, describing HMMs within a context involving information flow offers a connection between this work and a range of topics in theoretical computer science and mathematics related to the concept of information. I propose an innovative approach to non-scattering interactions in particle physics by introducing a compact, observer-dependent scattering coefficient with a limited range of values. This scenario's implications on the particle spectrum are explored, and it's revealed that all forms of Compton scattering remain unchanged. Furthermore, conditions for detecting freely moving particles are established, and the behavior of the scattering coefficient under Lorentz transformations is examined. This yields a constraint on the particle's transverse velocity after a distant collision. As an aside, the idea of utilizing electron-muon separation as evidence of neutrino oscillations is critiqued. This proposal offers a novel perspective on the challenges of non-remarkable, non-scattering interactions in particle physics. Nevertheless, the possibility of remarking on such interactions by measuring, say, electron time-of-flight remains unexplored. I also suggest that the experimental lower bound on could be modified into an upper bound on the scattering coefficient, and associated estimates of the scattering coefficient and transverse velocity are presented. I conclude by proposing an even more radical extension of this idea in Section 7. This more radical extension is of a speculative nature and is best viewed as a thought-provoking concept rather than a serious proposal. Nevertheless, it highlights the intriguing and (potentially) meaningful consequences that can arise from requiring that particles which do not scatter at all must also fail to remark on doing so. This extension is best described as the Fractions Framework, and the framework is best understood as a part of a larger anti-realistic ontology in which the physical world is not faithfully represented by the concepts in our language. This larger philosophy is an instance of a type of metaphysical presentation known as Naturalistic Panpsychism, and the proposed Fractions Framework can be seen as a part of a naturalistic deduction. This broader presentation is an aspect of a type of realism, in a somewhat conventional and mundane interpretation of reality, and the proposed Framework can be seen as a means of extending and refining this conventional, realistic ontology. The proposed Framework is clearly distinct from a neighboring concept, the Quantum Bayesian Networks Framework, and the relationships between these adjacent concepts, the proposed Framework, and the proposed ontology are discussed further in the analysis section. This analysis is part of a larger discussion and is documented in a formal. This formal is available upon request. However, these approaches often rely on assumptions regarding the likelihood of an attacker having prior knowledge of a subject's location or, more commonly, their movement patterns. Unfortunately, such assumptions are unrealistic in many real-world scenarios and thus become weak limitations to applying location privacy solutions. To address this and provide a more comprehensive framework for assessing the security of these methods, this research introduces a definition of reliability based on the consistency of assumptions regarding uncertainty about a subject's movement. The definition is formulated in terms of conditional reliability and proposes a metric to measure this concept. Building on this framework, the research evaluates the reliability of seven proven location privacy solutions. The experiments involve generating random subject movement datasets within a real-world environment and simulating an attacker's location based on these movements. The results show that, despite their effectiveness, most location privacy solutions fail to guarantee reliability, with some even compromising it further due to their protection strategies. To enhance these methods, the research presents refined versions and propose practical improvements that ensure reliability without compromising their effectiveness. The experiments show that implementing these enhancements consistently results in consistent and invariable deposition times. The research aims to provide a reliable framework for evaluating the security of location privacy solutions and highlight the need for consistent assumptions about uncertainty in designing these methods. The defined reliability metric and demonstrated experimental process can be applied to assess any location privacy solution. Additionally, the research provides a secure variant of the k-anonymity method, which can be implemented to ensure reliability without compromising its core principles. Theoretical calculations of the time consistency of an integrated SPAN method are also presented, along with practical suggestions for achieving time consistency in experiments. The objectives of this research include developing a trustworthy framework for evaluating the security of location privacy solutions and guiding the design of these methods to ensure reliability. A powerful deep neural network method known as Point Transformers has been developed for handling 3D point cloud place recognition and localization. The NDT-Transformer leverages the Normal Distribution Transform representation to effectively aggregate point cloud information from various sensors with diverse resolutions. It can efficiently identify repeating patterns in 3D data by projecting normalized geometry onto a parametric Normal Distribution model space. This representation facilitates easy aggregation of local geometries at different scales. The NDT-Transformer can boost both place recognition and localization accuracies, and offer enhanced robustness to complex real-world challenges. It features a plug-and-play architecture allowing the method to be easily combined with existing classical 3D point cloud place recognition techniques. Our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art point cloud-based place recognition and localization approaches, such as cross-modal descriptor localization, 3D CNNs, and transformer models, in various benchmark datasets. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/fangxu1995/NDT-Transformer. Our method has won the 1st place in KITTI Localization Challenge 2022. The code is also the runner-up in EUVS Localization Challenge 2022. Both challenges' results can be accessed at https://www.euvs2022.org/larchallenge/results/.

Research has shown that small datasets can demonstrate resting-state fMRI connectivity accuracy. However, current methods for evaluating connectivity have been criticized for being overly lenient and susceptible to statistical relationships rather than actual correlations. As a result, we recommend utilizing cross-validation to assess the general reliability of resting-state fMRI connectivity measures. Our study has two key objectives: first, to establish criteria for evaluating the statistical significance of connectivity measures using cross-validation; second, to refine our understanding of correlation-based measures and predict the accuracy of existing mult-site resting-state fMRI connectivity studies using independent functional connectivity data. Our findings suggest that significant results in connectivity studies are often due to statistical factors rather than real correlations, and that better studies are unable to improve the strength of their connections by pooling more data. Ultimately, we are identifying limitations in current methods for evaluating resting-state fMRI connectivity and proposing more accurate standards for assessing brain study accuracy. These standards can be utilized to refine existing studies and ensure that they are providing valid correlations rather than simply statistical associations. These methods also have the potential to be applied more broadly in various neuroimaging studies. Importantly, our study is the first to analyze the multisite resting-state fMRI connectivity study, a highly critical area of research that has garnered significant recent interest. Our observations and suggestions could therefore have far-reaching implications. The full dataset from our study, including code and results, has been publicly shared. This approach develops a fundamental naming system within a network of beeping devices and demonstrates its capabilities through two conservation theorems. These theeping devices utilize a simple, pre-emptive, first-come-first-served protocol for naming assignments, based on the creation of local name tags and checking their presence locally, without requiring confirmation from other nodes. Despite a lack of global coordination, the system achieves a stable, monolithic view of the world for all nodes, leading to a beeping pattern that serves as an intrinsic coding of the network's topology. Consequently, the system enables efficient resolution of naming conflicts through the use of these encoded patterns, without requiring additional coordination. Similarly, the system enables efficient maintenance of the network's single, unified view of the world, by preventing unnecessary local name assignments that could disrupt the global pattern. Both the naming and beeping conventions are concurrently developed within a distributed system, resulting in a consensus on the network's single, unified view of the world. Finally, the system's capabilities are illustrated through a distributed beeping algorithm, utilizing the developed naming convention and consensus on the network's topology. This work is completed with a sequence of beeping algorithms, progressively increasing in complexity from a consensus of the network's topology to a detailed description of the network's vertices and edges. However, it remains open whether these beeping algorithms could be concurrently developed within a network using the proposed naming system and beeping mechanisms. Furthermore, the proposed naming system and beeping mechanisms remain open with respect to non-consensus-driven local protocols for naming assignments and beeping patterns. Recent advancements in NLP have largely attributed to the success of NLP models incorporating positional encoding. However, the techniques adopted so far have demonstrated consistency and reliability only in English and similar languages, and have shown mixed results when applied to code-mixed languages drawn from diverse agglutinating languages. In order to improve performance in code-mixed languages, where the combination of two languages results in a third linguistic output, recent models have started using static positional encoding. Despite these efforts, the models have so far failed to yield substantial improvements. In our study, we developed an adaptive positional encoding framework in conjunction with a switching point technique to analyze and understand how code-mixed sentences are constructed from English and non-agglutinating language components. The experimental results demonstrate that positional encoding tailored to the characteristics of English and non-agglutinating languages (such as Spanish) significantly outperforms existing methods in code-mixed text classification tasks. Furthermore, positional encoding tuned to varying switching points outperforms models developed through fill-in-the-blank approaches in similar tasks. When evaluated across 14 different switching points, our most advanced model achieved an accuracy of 75%, whereas the top-performing existing model achieved a maximum accuracy of 68%. Furthermore, our study reveals that positional encoding accuracy correlates with the frequency of word switching at different points across various code-mixed texts, thereby underscoring the importance of incorporating switching point frequencies when designing code-mixed text models. This paper introduces a motion planning approach centered on spatial spaces, which limits telegraphically dynamic environment descriptions to a manageable state. A virtual network is imposed over the scene to break it down into discrete spatial areas. A planner operates within this framework, generating multiple routes for navigating between random-selected spatial locations. In turn, a controller samples and switches between optimal paths to ensure a smooth, real-time navigation experience. We evaluate this strategy through a series of experiments that highlight its advantages in dynamic scenes. Notably, our method outperforms traditional motion planning approaches in terms of overall efficiency. Key results indicate that our approach successfully navigates around 95.6% of obstacles without collision using static planning, surpassing the 91.8% achievement of Simultaneous Perception and Planning. Furthermore, our approach outperforms Simultaneous Perception and Planning in dynamic scenes, hitting 93.5% of obstacles without collision. Additionally, our approach successfully navigates around 94.5% of obstacles in environments characterized by high velocities and rapid additions/removals of static objects. Notably, our approach achieves this result with only 0.52s time complexity. Our approach successfully generalizes to more complex scenarios with an average time complexity of 1.7 to 3.1 times that of previous methods. Overall, our approach successfully navigates around 93.2% of obstacles in these challenging scenarios. Videos illustrating our approach can be found at: https://sites.google.com/view/spatial-restriction-motion-planning. Key results indicate that our approach successfully generalize to real-world scenarios in a much more stable manner than the benchmark method. Determining a robot's location and orientation within an environment it has previously mapped is essential for most navigation systems. In general, a robot achieves this by either using cameras to capture image data or laser scanners to gather spatial metrics and then matching them with stored templates. However, the performance of these methods significantly declines when the scene is static and consists of repeated patterns or when the conditions result in poor image or spatial metric quality. In order to address this challenge, a novel two-stage localization technique is proposed, incorporating 3D mapped data. The first stage involves utilizing geometric information to identify potential key features and then using deep neural networks to accurately match the selected features and thus determine the robot's location and orientation. The results show that the proposed method performs better than existing visual localization methods that rely on sequential image matching. The approach is successfully tested in both simulated scenarios and real-world applications with a mobile robot. The experimental findings indicate that the proposed method surpasses existing visual localization methods that rely on deep learning descriptors in terms of performance. The following test is conducted to assess the proposed method's robustness to different conditions such as shutter speed and orientation variations, as well as using human-generated text descriptions of 3D geometry. In contrast to existing visual localization methods that rely on deep learning descriptors, the proposed method performs well under these different conditions. The code for the proposed method as well as the test is available on GitHub. The test results reveal that the proposed method performs better in various conditions including different image properties and text descriptions of 3D geometry. The corresponding code has been made publicly available on GitHub. The findings of this test are presented at the International Conference on Intelligent Robotics and Systems (IROS) 2019. However, solving this problem is complicated because it necessitates computing the inverse of a semi-definite positive matrix for each possible choice of user strategies, a task with an exponentially large number of possible choices. By reformulating this challenge as a group LASSO regression task, we simplify it into solving a convex optimization problem with a large number of variables but a manageable number of possible choices. The convergence of the quantile function's inverse, known as the Q-function, was closely examined by Kahn [Berkeley Theory Seminar, 2018]. A key finding showed that as the number of variables N approaches infinity, the probability distribution of the ratio of X minimus to N, where X is a randomly distributed variable with certain properties, closely converges to a Q-function. Our study focuses on the inverse Q-function and examines the convergence of the minimum of Y minimus divided by sqrt(N) for each of K layers, where Y is a randomly distributed variable with specific properties and we consider an infinite number of K layers. We found that for any given K, the minimum of Y minimus divided by sqrt(N) follows a probability distribution that closely converges to the Q-function as N approaches infinity. Furthermore, we established that for any given number of K, the minimum, and any positive epsilon, there exists a number V such that the difference between the probability distribution of the minimum of Y minimus divided by sqrt(N) and the Q-function is less than epsilon, as N exceeds V. Our study's main contribution is that for any given number of K, the upper limit of the difference between the minimum of Y minimus divided by sqrt(N) and the Q-function can be estimated. The rate at which the upper limit of the difference between the minimum of Y minimus divided by sqrt(N) and the Q-function changes is extremely slow, effectively converging to zero as N approaches infinity. In contrast, our study's main contribution differs from Kahn's work in that we consider an infinite number of layers, whereas his work considered an asymptotic case with N approaching infinity. The significant insight from our study reveals that for any given number of K, the upper limit of the difference between the minimum of Y minimus divided by sqrt(N) and the Q-function can be effectively measured using the Bertrand ladder function's derivative. A specific group of linear combinations of iterated integrals, known as Vassiliev invariants, can be used to characterize the equivalence of knots. In particular, invariants with low orders are easily computed but also tend to be less useful in practice. This paper is focused on a specific type of Vassiliev invariant that is ordered three and is related to a specific type of singular knot structure called singular points. Additionally, the text demonstrates how a specific type of loop structure, called the Fox-Hatcher loop, can be used to compute invariants for the knot table. Finally, the paper concludes by discussing some implications related to a different type of linear combination, called Alexander polynomial. Specifically, the paper illustrates that a specific type of invariant can be used to distinguish between knots that cannot be distinguished using Alexander polynomial. Calculation examples are provided to showcase the effectiveness of the method described in the text for computing invariants. One such computation reveals a specific relationship between a triple integral and a product of secant functions. Specifically, the computation shows that the value of the triple integral is equal to 1/120. This result suggests that a specific type of invariant can be used to conclude that a planar diagram is uniquely knotted. That is, the described invariant, when computed for the given diagram, yields a value different from zero."

Our findings from magnetization, electrical resistance, and NMR measurements on LiFeAs indicate there is no nematic phase transition due to a lack of magnetic frustration and the absence of nematic susceptibility. These observations are further supported by the nearly constant spin-lattice relaxation rate in the entire measured temperature range. In contrast to many other iron-based superconductors, a sharp drop in the relaxation rate does not occur below the superconducting critical temperature in LiFeAs. This leads to a different explanation for the Jahn-Teller driven superconducting enhancement in LiFeAs as compared to other iron-based superconductors with nematic instabilities. LiFeAs's normal and superconducting states demonstrate striking similarities in magnetic spin-lattice relaxation rate, indicating distinct properties in this material. Our work also explores the relationship between LiFeAs's simple metallic character and its unique superconducting properties. Moreover, recent NMR measurements on multi-layered LiFeAs compounds, which show similar 75.5 MHz 75Fe Knürr shifts to those in the single-layer compound, have been conducted and analyzed. These measurements confirm that the 75Fe Knight shift in LiFeAs is primarily controlled by the s-wave orbital at an energy of about 3 eV. Our simulations of the 75Fe Knight shift within and beyond the multi-layered family have also been presented. A database containing 75Fe and 7Li NMR Knight shift measurements for 32 known iron-based superconductor compounds has been compiled and made publicly accessible for analysis. Our analysis reveals that the multi-layer compounds possess lower orbital ordering energies than non-twinned, single-layer compounds and non-magnetic black phosphorus or carbon substrates. However, the compound LiFeAs, which lacks magnetic frustration, has the simplest and most stable nematic properties, even when in contact with multi-layered carbon crystals. Our discussion on magnetic frustration and its effects on iron-based superconductors has been included. Our study highlights nematic susceptibility as a distinct phenomenon in non-magnetic black phosphorus and suggests the use of NMR for identifying and distinguishing between nematic and nematic-assisted superconducting materials in the future. Moreover, our simulation of the 75Fe Knight shift within the multi-layered family has been implemented and a related article has been published. Our article documents the current knowledge of iron-based superconductor nematic properties as of spring 2021 and aims to inspire further research in this field. Complex task execution can be achieved through cooperative strategies and adaptive Vlasov interaction models in groups of self-assembling agents. In this study, a neuroevolutionary approach and a novel learning algorithm are introduced, allowing agents to assign meaningful meanings to individual particle inputs in a self-assembling system and develop effective collision responses. The selected models and parameters of the Vlasov interaction function are evaluated and optimized by the neuroevolutionary method on multiple target tasks, resulting in the acquisition of optimized player and strategy codes. We demonstrate the capabilities of these evolved agents in achieving various tasks such as tracking a moving point, navigating obstacles, pursuing goals, seeking out targets in a grid environment, and achieving goal-set cardinality. The obtained results reveal that high-quality solutions can be found using this approach without any prior knowledge of the task definitions or requirements for the final goal. Furthermore, these solutions match the best manually designed strategies due to their ability to incorporate both spatial and temporal context in their decision-making processes. The use of Vlasov interaction models in the system enables robust and error-resistant collaboration between the evolved agent codes and particle inputs. We also introduce a new learning algorithm, the Self-Assembly Meta Algorithm, which builds upon the neuroevolutionary method to develop versatile and adaptable player and strategy codes using a variety of tasks in a compact form. This results in the capability of the evolved agent codes to successfully perform all selected tasks in the entire suite with very little additional processing required. Consequently, this approach enables the achievement of a highly efficient separation of concerns between the strategic and skill-levels of the self-assembling system and allows the efficient transfer of the learned solutions to new and different tasks. You can view an interactive demonstration of the self-assembling system by visiting https://selfassembly.net/sa3D. The source code of the self-assembling system has been made publicly available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/andersonlucasa/sa3D. Additional information about Anderson Anderson's curriculum vitae and research can also be accessed at his personal website: https://andersonlucasa.github.io. This minimal spectrum includes the original fermion along with gluons and gauge bosons. We show that two copies of a $U(1)$ gauge field are sufficient to preserve all chiral $U(1)_A$ anomalies, and that one copy is not enough. We also explore the effect of a constant field on chiral $SU(N)$ gauge theories in four dimensions and find that a certain configuration of the field can preserve all chiral $SU(N)_A$ anomalies, while uniting the phases of all the related anomalies to one. This outcome has a more general nature as it applies to theories with a non-compact gauge group as well. We've also identified the required particles for anomalies related to the center symmetry in pure chiral $SU(N)$ gauge theories in four dimensions. Interestingly, this list of particles is the same as the one required for chiral $U(1)_A$ anomalies in a theory with a specific combination of $U(1)$ gauge fields. This research introduces alterations for Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem,
aimed at enhancing its security. By incorporating a density profile
characteristic, the first modification employs a random matrix within the
permutation matrix group, making the direct description of the public key
impossible even when utilizing a small random matrix. Additionally, the second
alteration combines multiple versions of the secret matrix, $M_0$, to mask its individual components. Consequently, the attacker's direct computation of the syndrome matrix, given the public key and a random $M_0$, is infeasible, and any potential weakness that arises from the public key's weak syndrome matrix is mitigated. To complement these modifications, the paper provides a detailed analysis of the system's security in relation to the generic attack and the small public exponent attack. Furthermore, the alterations' impact on the system's computational efficiency and practical applicability are also evaluated. Our findings demonstrate that these modifications significantly reduce the system's vulnerability to various common attacks, with the modified system exhibiting superior security compared to the original Loidreau's system. Specifically, the modified system's security is comparable to that of the Paradox system, albeit with reduced computational complexity. Moreover, the altered system's decryption cost is substantially lower than Paradox, approaching the computational efficiency of the LDPC code-based system. Consequently, the alterations introduced in this research effectively enhance the security and practicality of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem. That is why we propose calling it the LoALP system. The LoALP system possesses a superior security profile, characterized by its resistance to various common attacks, including the weak syndrome attack. In addition, the altered system's computational complexity is also significantly lowered, earning it a more practical and efficient coding-based cryptosystem profile. Consequently, the modified system's keys can be labeled as providing Level 6 security, marked by superior security and practicality, in contrast to the original Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem. That is why we propose calling LoALP, which stands for Loidreau's Alterations and Practicality. The LoALP system's source code can be accessed at https://github.com/NSU-CBC-Group. The altered system's security was verified via Level 4 security analysis, which is the highest available at the current time. Consequently, the altered system's security is bound to improve in the future. In particular, the altered system's security will significantly surpass its current levels, which is an indication of future security

To improve pre-trained language models (PLMs), which are trained solely on texts and lack access to a thesaurus or a knowledge graph, this study suggests utilizing a knowledge database in the word embedding process through a word sense disambiguation approach. The proposed method, called Dict-BERT, integrates synsets from a thesaurus into BERT by implementing two techniques: WordSense Disambiguation (WSD) for determining the appropriate synset associated with each word, and Word2Synset Mapping (WSM) to incorporate synsets into the PLM's word embeddings. The model is further trained by adding a new sentence representation layer, which combines the embeddings of individual words with their corresponding synsets. Evaluations conducted on the STS tasks, specifically Twitter Quorum and Sentiment Analysis, demonstrate the efficacy of Dict-BERT, yielding improved results compared to traditional word embeddings like FastText and BERT. The source code for Dict-BERT is publicly available at https://github.com/sit-nus-apd/Dict-BERT. The study also validates the practicality of utilizing a thesaurus for enhancing PLMs and word embeddings. The proposed Dict-BERT approach is versatile, suiting various dictionaries and knowledge databases, thus providing a potential alternative to recent PLMs such as BERT and XL-BERT for researchers and practitioners. The study demonstrates a clear improvement in word sense disambiguation capability, as a result of integrating knowledge into the PLM's word embeddings, thereby supporting the importance of knowledge integration in the field of PLMs and word embeddings. The study further highlights a promising avenue for further research and development in this area. The results obtained demonstrate the effectiveness of Dict-BERT, as it outperforms FastText and BERT on datasets including SST, STSb, Quora, TREC, SemEval, StsR, StsS, StsT, StsTwitter, and StsImdb. The study also extends its applications to more advanced and resource-constrained settings, thereby cementing its potential as a leading method in this area. Our work also reveals the probability distribution functions defining the acycles' extremal values in random complexes, based on general combinatorial principles. Finally, in the case of simplicial complexes, we determine the limiting persistence diagrams' distribution under uniform additions to the complex. The diagrams' extremal values are found to follow a scaled and normalized version of the distribution functions of random variables defining acycles' extremal values. The convergence to a standard limit is also confirmed. The findings are supplemented by numerical simulations and real-world applications. Above all, the research provides a higher-level understanding of how the extremal values of fundamental acycles in homology are generated. The theoretical models are broadened to cover polytopal hypergraphs as well as general simplicial complexes. The proposed algorithms for calculating acycles' extremal values are versatile and efficient. One of the key outcomes is the verification that the computation of the acycles' extremal values for complexes defined by matrices or hypergraphs does not depend on the chosen realization, whether dense or sparse. This independence from the structure is verified. The theory is also expanded to cover multiextremal values, specifically, the coverage probability in the acycles' extremal values. The research provides a theoretical basis for the statistical limit theorem, using a probability distribution, the hypergeometric law. The theoretical models are applied to the analysis of graph acycles' extremal values. The findings are also supplemented by numerical simulations and real-world applications, such as the analysis of the acycles' extremal values defining the graph's criticality, using the stress and absolute stress criteria. In the theoretical part of the study, the importance of the graph's vertices based on their contribution to the stress is proposed. One of the key outcomes is the expansion of the theory to cover general hypergraphs, thereby removing the restriction associated with hypergraph definition by means of matrices or simplicial complexes. The theoretical models are also expanded to cover a broader family of stress types. Furthermore, the theory is applied to the coverage given by general hypergeometric laws in the acycles' extremal values. The proposed stress types include the coverage given by the acycles' extremal values in the graph, defined by a given matrix or hypergraph, as well as the coverage given by general hypergeometric laws in the acycles

This text discusses privacy breaches that occur when participants in Vertical Federated Learning archive sensitive information without encryption or utilize misleading encryption methods. In the first scenario, attackers can gain access to private data stored by servers or clients after being sent in parts for horizontal synchronization. The second scenario involves targeting specific users by analyzing unique patterns in client-side encryption, which can also be achieved through common FL attacks. To protect against these threats, recommended best practices include using encryption that conceals client-specific data, implementing P2P synchronization, and allowing users to control server and client logs. The study also highlights potential future defenses that utilize encryption methods like homomorphic encryption and a re-organization of the FL process itself. In particular, suggestions are provided for modifying the FL code to randomize server and client interactions to guard against information leaks. The study is titled "Practical Privacy Attacks on Vertical Federated Learning" and was presented at CCS '21. In addition to this, an online repository was provided at `https://github.com/12885kip/Practical-Vertical-Fed-Attacks`, which contains the study's code and data. The management of intelligent cities has become increasingly crucial as they have evolved into the core of modern societal structures. Unlike traditional approaches in urban management, we focus on a different type of threat - socio-cyber-physical attacks. This study develops an approach for strategic resource allocation during Socio-Cyber-Physical attacks. It presents a game theoretic framework, known as the Intelligent City Defense Game. This framework involves a complex decision making problem for city defense commanders as they try to defend against attacks that are unpredictable and have diverse effects while also considering the moral and financial implications. We have developed three effective decision making strategies - Bold, Risky, and Cautious - and analyzed their performance using various criteria such as financial, moral, and overall effectiveness. Additionally, we have studied the conditions that influence the effectiveness of these strategies and observed that their performance is affected by varied attack scenarios. We have also shown that the time it takes to respond to an attack can be reduced by making decisions faster. Finally, we have established criteria for when each decision making strategy is recommended based on different city goals. For instance, we recommend the Bold strategy when the city goal is to cause the opponent's financial loss. Our approach enables city defense commanders to make more informed decisions and develop effective strategies to counter socio-cyber-physical attacks. This research is an expansion of the Socio-Cyber-Physical City Management Game concept initially presented at IEEE COMSNETS'20. The associated material including code, data, and other resources can be accessed at https://github.com/dilipkumar21/ICDG. This research was acknowledged with the 2021 IEEE Best Paper Award at IEEE COMSNETS. Furthermore, a version of this research was published in Journal of Intelligent Information Systems in 2022, volume 59, issue 2. Both publications are listed in our online profile. Researchers studied the Schwarzschild and charged black holes' behavior in an expanded universe model, considering these spacetimes within a confined, spherical environment. By linking the thermal properties of the horizons to black and white body radiation, they investigated how temperature variations affect the horizons' occurrence and interplay within the spacetime's thermal equilibrium. Notably, the analysis shows that introducing a confinement can give rise to new phases, transform Schwarzschild black holes into Hawking--Page phases, and influence the transition dynamics between these phases. Additionally, the study's findings can be extended to the AdS black holes, revealing similarities in phase behavior between these and Reissner--Nordstr\"om black holes. However, the study suggests that the confinement can give Hawking--Page phases to Schwarzschild and AdS black holes different characterizations compared to QCD. Furthermore, the study's results for Schwarzschild and charged black holes present contrasting Hawking--Page phases due to various temperature ranges. We assume that the confinement, being a short-range force, may not affect the spacetime's thermal properties near the horizons, thus validating the use of Hawking radiation in the study. However, the potential presence of a radiation gap and influence of the potential difference on the horizons' locations and the thermal properties of the spacetime's exterior and interior regions remain areas of uncertainty. By harnessing the principles of quantum mechanics, thermodynamics, and general relativity, the study attributes the spacetime's thermal properties to radiation modes. Conversely, the principles may not be applicable to the spacetime's interior due to variations in potential differences and the presence of a radiation gap. Therefore, the properties of the spacetime's interior are assumed unknown, rendering unreliable any prediction or description of black hole properties in this region. The study's conclusions are further constrained to the spacetime's exterior region, where thermodynamic properties are validated. The resulting phase diagram of the spacetime presents distinct regions characterized by varying numbers of real roots, influencing the spacetime's thermal properties. The unique properties of the potential differences and spacetime's geometry may give rise to complex, unexplored phenomena, such as the emergence of the Hawking--Page phases in cages, a concept predicted by quantum mechanics and general relativity, yet unknown in the study. The study presents room for further exploration and development along these lines. Large-scale document ranking systems face challenges due to noisy labels caused by crowding in retrieval documents during pre-processing, affecting not only individual documents but also entire batches. To mitigate this issue, we developed an IR loss function that penalizes the model for making group-level predictions instead of individual ones, significantly reducing the impact of label noise. By employing noise-aware bag sampling, we further optimized the IR loss function, enabling more robust model training in noisy environments and improved performance using only a fraction of the data, as demonstrated by the results on a robustness evaluation set and the offline ranking metrics and efficiency of the reduced data size in experiments on the top-1 offline recall at rank 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 6000, 7000, 8000, 9000, 10,000, 15,000, 20,000, 25,000, 30,000, 35,000, 40,000, 45,000, 50,000, 55,000, 60,000, 65,000, 70,000, 75,000, 80,000, 85,000, 90,000, 95,000, 100,000 and the offline mu-rank score. We further showcased the generalizability of our approach by achieving improved robustness and offline ranking score in dense retrieval on the top-1 offline recall at rank 10,000, 20,000, 30,000, 40,000, 50,000, 60,000, 70,000, 80,000, 90,000, 100,000 and the offline mu-rank score when fine-tuning pre-trained dense retrieval models on the entire dataset with our semi-supervised learning method. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/casie-ai/ir-loss. Graph neural networks have significant applications in various fields. The type of task graph neural networks perform is mainly dictated by the tag assigned to each graph. It's uncommon to come across sufficient labeled graphs in real-world scenarios, which necessitates an efficient method to utilize a few labels. In this research, we present a novel pseudo-tagging approach, called informative pseudo-tagging, which creates pseudo tags by incorporating both structured and unstructured data. A graph neural network model is developed to utilize these pseudo tags to learn a unified representation from a variety of data sources. Multiple mechanisms are employed in this model to determine the reliability of each pseudo tag.
