Object identification is a crucial component of computer vision, involving both object detection and name recognition. The object detection stage involves identifying objects within an image while also determining their locations. In object identification, bicycles and cars are considered the same object class, despite differing in location. Presently, most advanced object identification models are deep neural networks-based and trained in a closed vocabulary setting due to a shortage of training samples, where a single object class can encompass multiple location labels, such as "car" being associated with "front", "rear", etc. In this paper, a pseudo-label method is proposed to address the absent location labels in object identification. This method utilises a primary network to generate location-predicted labels which are then imparted to a secondary network for further refinement. Experimental outcomes validate the efficacy of this approach, setting a new benchmark for open-vocabulary object identification by achieving an average degradation of 0.7% box AP, 3.2% box AR@100, 5.3% attribute AR@100, and 6.0% metadata AR@100 compared to the baseline without pseudo-labels. The proposed method not only applies to object identification but also identification tasks as well. The proposed method has been successfully applied to an open-vocabulary identification pipeline where images are first located using a pre-trained model, and then named using a text regression model. This method outperformed other pipeline approaches, achieving an average degradation of 1.4% box AP, 4.1% box AR@100, 5.8% attribute AR@100, and 6.4% metadata AR@100 compared to the baseline without pseudo-labels. The proposed method sets a new standard in open-vocabulary identification and can be used to solve other visual identification tasks. One significant challenge in neural architecture search (NAS) lies in efficiently sampling a diverse range of valid architectures to train, as most methods attempt to mitigate alignment between the distribution of valid architectures and that of potentially superior ones. Another issue arises from high training costs for the top-performing architectures. In this paper, we seek to address these problems by studying the characteristics of NAS datasets, specifically by examining the influence of category diversity and imbalance within the dataset 'CIFAR'. Additionally, we present an innovative method known as reduction-guided architecture search (RGAS) to tackle the NAS training bias. RGAS involves a new selection scheme for cells to train, which leverages a current cell's capacity for predicting its own parameters and, in conjunction with parameter sharing, deliberately forces weak cells to handle more parameters, thereby accelerating weight learning in top-performing cells. In contrast, our new selection scheme simply samples cells randomly, forcing weak cells to handle fewer parameters. As a result, our method can efficiently train top-performing cells while reducing the massive cost associated with the search space, and it happens so quickly that it only needs one stage. In experiments conducted on the 'CIFAR' dataset, our model achieved a remarkable 84.4% top-1 accuracy after the first stage, eventually reaching 85.44% top-1 accuracy upon completing the second stage. In addition to this, our model achieved a 9-time speedup over the standard two-stage approach. In summary, our reduction-guided architecture search offers a highly efficient solution to the NAS bias by only requiring one stage to start learning top-performing cells, thereby making it highly suitable for efficient architecture search. Time series analysis is a crucial area in statistics and data science, involving the graphical examination of time series data to identify patterns, anomalies, and correlations. There are limited, published approaches for the visual inspection of time series data. We have developed a comprehensive R package named theft, aimed at providing straightforward, visual tools to support the in-depth analysis of statistical time series and the automatic detection of anomalies. This package goes beyond simple time series plots by offering a sophisticated, multi-feature visual inspection system inspired by the Feature Driven Statistical Methodology. We have generated various real-world datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of our thear functions, offering a superior alternative to the shwts function in the tsdiag package. Our package is available under an open-source license and can be easily installed using the CRAN network and Git Hub repositories. We have included supplementary material, including our generated datasets and the corresponding code, at Git Hub. We are committed to continually improving and expanding the capabilities of the theft package to cater to diverse statistical time series needs. We welcome users to submit new feature suggestions to enhance the package's functionality. To better understand the purpose and structure of the thear functions, we have adopted a consistent naming convention, combining three elements: the prefix "thear" indicating a statistical tool for time series analysis, followed by the type of feature being presented (e.g., "raw" for raw data, "det" for detrended data, "diff" for differeenced data, "log" for data transformed to a logarithmic scale, and "med" for data transformed to a median value at each period), and the specific feature being analyzed (denoted in bold). Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an extensively utilized method that translates sentence-by-sentence evaluations into a reliability score. This score indicates the degree of accuracy in a translator's work, however, the conventional method of assessing reliability through peer review is costly and time-consuming. To resolve this issue, we have developed a new Bayesian method to estimate a translator's level of proficiency (reliability) using a limited number of annotations derived from peer review, while simultaneously accounting for potential subjective aspects of TQA evaluations. To facilitate this process, we have created a simulated dataset representing diverse real-world scenarios and utilized a Shiny app to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for calculating a translator's reliability score. Additionally, we have compared our Bayesian method to a competing machine learning approach, showing that our approach outperforms it in most scenarios. Notably, when confronted with a simulated scenario resembling a 5-hour evaluation, the error margin of our proposed method remains less than 0.1, indicating that the Bayesian method surpasses the performance of the machine learning approach in nearly all evaluated scenarios. Furthermore, the source code for our method is publicly available at the repository https://github.com/mindseries/TQA-Bayes. future work is also discussed in the paper. Consequently, future studies should center on expanding the peer review dataset rather than concentrating on a single assessment. To achieve this goal, we recommend the implementation of a straightforward annotation scheme to make peer review more efficient, and we also suggest to develop semi or fully automated methods to assess TQA evaluations. Moreover, we propose that professional translators engage in rewriting tasks, and we have begun a preliminary investigation showing that using these rewritten texts can effectively enhance the estimation of translator proficiency. Despite the importance of auditing, categorization is a challenging task due to the need to balance between thoroughness and practicality. If the categories are too broad, the resulting analysis might overlook crucial details, whereas narrowly defined categories might lead to information overload and missed opportunities. Moreover, the need to adapt categorization models to diverse systems often renders existing models ineffective. This study proposes the use of formal concept analysis as a framework for categorization, allowing for systematized categorization and the detection of shadow entities – entities that appear only in single occasions. To address the issue of unknown attributes, which hinders users' ability to pose queries, we suggest leveraging Dempster-Shafer theory to estimate the presence or absence of attributes. Finally, we outline a strategy for auditing departments within information security organizations using both formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shafer theory. With formal concept analysis, we can discover hidden entities and understand the inherent dynamics of the system, whereas Dempster-Shafer theory allows us to tackle the issue of unknown attributes and obtain a more accurate picture of the system. In reliable networks, sudden disruptions to communication services can be predicted and prepared for through advanced failure detection mechanisms.  These mechanisms ensure quick detection of problems, enabling swift switches to alternative routes and minimizing outages for critical systems.  Beyond the network itself, similar reliability features are found in other critical areas, such as power grids and transportation systems, which however fall short in a crucial aspect of software updates for IoT devices.  The current approach to updating IoT codes lacks a standardized process that guarantees a stable and stable environment for testing and implementation.  Consequently, numerous bugs and security vulnerabilities are left exposed during the testing phase, which may remain unresolved even after the update is complete.  Therefore, this paper will conduct a comprehensive study of the popular Wi-SUN mesh network used in smart cities, Smart grids and other systems, which will involve collecting and analysing firmware logs from real-world devices following a change in their network configuration, in order to measure the effect of firmware updates on these devices and shed light on the common issues related to such updates, as well as to provide recommendations for optimizing these transitions and reducing risks.  The results from our research reveal the practical problems that arise during updates, which show a significant correlation between these issues and the specific update method employed, with certain techniques generating more errors than others.  The findings from our study will contribute positively towards creating a better understanding of dependent systems and their need for efficient updates and fault detection mechanisms, which will also shed some light on possible solutions to these problems and their effects on IoT communication. Furthermore, the fractal dimension exhibits a continuous shift of $\Delta l_0 = W/12$ in response to changes in the disorder, where $W$ represents the system's bandwidth and $\Delta l_0$ is a characteristic scale of the shift. We show that this shift can be attributed to a delocalized precursor that exists even in the delocalized phase and partially survives in the localized phase, where it exerts a disproportionate influence on low-energy local observables. We observe that the fractal dimension's form remains consistent across different systems and is independent of the system's specifics, indicating that this precursor's effects are widespread. Using this discovery, we develop a theoretical model for the fractal dimension's behavior in systems that exhibit complex behavior with multiple interactions. We find that this model aligns with our data and predicts that the fractal dimension's maximum value is achievable in systems with complex behavior and multiple interactions. A novel approach to radio frequency (RF) power prediction has been introduced, relying on empirical data and specialized machine learning algorithms. It is demonstrated that RF power measurements can be effectively generated through a combination of spatial analysis and temporal forecasting, combining open-source geographic information systems with advanced time-series prediction techniques. Furthermore, this method assesses the influence of uneven terrain, water bodies, and urban development on signal strength. As a result, this approach reduces reliance on proprietary site survey tools and empirical models for RF power estimation. To facilitate seamless machine learning-based RF power prediction, a detailed dataset featuring characteristics such as time, geometry, and radio frequency signal strength is transmitted from base stations to mobile devices. Utilizing these maps as input, a deep convolutional neural network can produce predictive models of RF power levels across entire cities with virtually no need for manual site surveying. Experimental results indicate that these models accurately forecast RF power levels across 10 cities in the United States, reducing the average error rate to less than 3.0 decibels for frequencies above 6 GHz. Given the rapid increase in 5G frequencies, this approach holds significant practical value for establishing robust and error-free cellular networks. It is our intention that this research will inspire further development of machine-learnable neural models, potentially leading to completely empirical RF power prediction methods in the future. The source code for this project, including all datasets and code, can be accessed at https://github.com/black23rd/Deep-RF-Power.

In the context of power system modeling, our study reveals that integrating specific elements has a profound effect on the system's overall performance. We analyzed two widely used models in the US: the National Energy Modelling System (NEMS) and the Regional Energy Decision (REDD) model, focusing on the impact of generating technologies on the system's behavior. We observed that the integration of specific generator types significantly influences the optimal path of resource selection, capital cost estimates, and the calculated social rate of return. Our analysis also highlights the fragility of model outcomes to assumptions and points to the need for uniform methodologies in model design. Ultimately, our work aims to improve the precision and objectivity of power system modeling. 

In terms of quantitative analysis, our research shows that varying the input assumptions of certain parameters results in accurate predictions of key performance indicators both within and beyond the initially assumed range. This outcome is largely attributed to the optimal algorithm's inherent flexibility. We also found that the numerical solution of a related non-linear program tends to favor scenarios with lower costs over those with higher costs. 

The methodological aspect of our study holds broader applicability as it can be applied to various power system models to evaluate their responsiveness. Our approach can be employed as a tool in model design to gauge the impact of specific policy choices or technological developments on power supply systems. 

Conversely, our research indicates that the numerical solution of a power system model often prioritizes scenarios with greater energy production, lower capital expenditures, and lower risks. This bias might be attributed to the algorithmic preferences of the computational method or the built-in characteristics of the power system itself. Further investigation is required to determine the source of this effect. In model design, this bias should be acknowledged and the associated assumptions refined. 

Lastly, our study reveals that the power system model is more resilient than the econometric model. Although both models demonstrate high responsiveness, our analysis suggests that the econometric model exhibits more precise predictions. 

In terms of policy recommendations, our research encourages the integration of sensitive elements in power supply models and points to the need for uniform design methodologies and thorough assumption verification. Additionally, our work implies that the US energy models can accurately forecast key performance indicators both within and beyond the initially assumed range. Ultimately, our analysis underscores the significance of methodology and assumption importance in power system modeling design.

The current trend in 3D detection from LiDAR and camera data involves using separate neural networks to extract features, which are then combined and trained in an end-to-end manner. However, this method is complicated by difficulties in coordinating the two networks and aligning their differing feature maps. Furthermore, training such a network requires vast computational resources. 

In response, we present the BEVFusion framework, which simplifies feature fusion through beam fusion and coordinate transformation, thereby reducing coordination complexities and aligning feature scales. Moreover, by transforming LiDAR features into a beam map, we are able to reduce the high-dimensional LiDAR data and integrate the two sensors in a more balanced manner. 

Results show that the BEVFusion framework significantly outperforms previous methods across various scenes and significantly reduces inference time by combining the computational efficiencies of LiDAR and camera sensors. Specifically, we demonstrate a notable 2.3 m mean average precision improvement in the NuScenes dataset at an 50% recall rate compared to the previous state-of-the-art. The code for the BEVFusion framework is available at https://github.com/ruki-y/kendoo.

The need arises for aggregating streaming data, performing distributed calculations, and triggering actions on data streams to create valuable insights. We propose an open-source platform called H-STREAM that demonstrates a unified approach to processing big data streams and historical data in a distributed environment, enabling the creation and execution of complex analytics pipelines. We showcase the platform's capabilities with multiple pipeline configurations that employ diverse querying and data transformation techniques. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of H-STREAM using two real-time data sets in experiments conducted across six nodes. The results reveal the system's efficacy in handling big data streams and historical data, while achieving fast query processing through query parallelization. Detecting these particles, primarily produced through the same process as their standard model counterparts but potentially influenced by new physics, can be complicated. Recent research has focused on the single production process of top and bottom partners, revealing both resonant and non-resonant production methods. While the resonant approach is straightforward, the non-resonant pathway is more intricate and needs detailed analyses. This study provides a comprehensive review of the non-resonant single production of top and bottom partners, discussing the main features of each partner's properties that can be deduced from this process. Additionally, this work presents simplified models that illustrate key aspects of the non-resonant production mechanisms. Finally, this work presents specific predictions for various types of high-mass standard model particles. The growing web dataset of knowledge is beneficial for language translation tasks but poses challenges to existing machine translation models. Traditional methods relying on raw text fail to effectively utilize knowledge base data, leading to decreased translation quality and increased confusion. In language pairs involving knowledge base data, standard neural machine translation models struggle to handle knowledge-related words and sentences. This paper introduces a groundbreaking method called Copy System (CS) to incorporate knowledge base data. CS maintains a separate memory buffer for knowledge-related words and employs a copy mechanism to directly input these words into translations. Furthermore, CS employs a sophisticated attention mechanism to unify knowledge and general memories. Through systematic evaluations and fine-tuning, CS is shown to significantly outperform the baseline on both simple and complex SPARQL translation tasks and real-world data sets. Additionally, CS is proven to surpass state-of-the-art models and perform on par with manual interventions of renowned SPARQL translation models. Moreover, CS achieves a record-breaking improvement in knowledge-related translation accuracy and overall translation efficiency. Utilizing knowledge-related words to translate is a pioneering concept in the neural machine translation field, and CS showcases its efficacy through empirical results. The proposed model is expected to set a new standard for translating knowledge base data in the SPARQL language, ultimately contributing to the SPARQL conjugation pursuit. It is demonstrated that a Nichols algebra over a traditional Weyl group $W$ with rank greater than 1, classified under Type A, has a rank equal to the group's order, with specific (p, p') ordering. This verifies a hypothesis outlined in a prior study by the same authors. Meanwhile, a formula for calculating the rank of a Nichols algebra over a finite p-group $G$, with \p is not equal to p', has been derived. Moreover, for any finite p-group $G$, with \p not equal to p', there exists a conventional sub-group $W$ with a rank greater than 1, such that the order of its Nichols algebra is the group's order, with a specified (p, p') ordering. This result invalidates the applicability of an existing conjecture related to Ding's classification theorem. In addition, it is proven that if the characteristic of an algebra is a prime number and the Koszul dimension of a graded Nichols algebra is greater than 1, then the algebra is classical. This result strengthens an already published theorem. Lastly, it is established that if the algebra's rank in accordance with Ding's classification can be paired with its Koszul dimension, then the algebra is classical. This result further validates a previously published conjecture. Several examples are given to illustrate that various conjectures mentioned above do not hold for infinite p-groups or algebras. One significant implication is that the conjectures mentioned above are only applicable to finite p-groups or algebras with a rank equal to the group's or algebra's order, with a specified (p, p') ordering. In addition, it is observed that the conjectures do not hold for groups or algebras with a rank equal to 1. To achieve these goals, cohomology classes in conjugacy Burnside modules are employed, using techniques from commutative algebra and Gorenstein-Knapp's method. The primary methods used here provide novel applications to study Nichols algebras over groups with a rank greater than 1 or infinite groups, with these techniques potentially being useful in other areas. In addition, it is noted that the primary techniques used here are distinct from those used in recent studies by the same authors. The study is completed by listing 41 unverified conjectures in the area of study. Several significant questions related to these conjectures are also raised. Graph normalization, a widely applied technique in graph machine learning, has been found to enhance model resilience and learning stability. Most current implementations of graph normalization follow an iterative approach, beginning by computing node scores or subgraph weights, with the aim of maximizing these scores or subgraph weights. This approach can lead to unrealistic outcomes in which all nodes are assigned a score of zero or a single graph node forms an MISP (Maximum Weight Independent Set). This issue is particularly evident in scenarios involving complex graphs. To address this limitation, we introduce the concept of iterative graph normalization, where the scale of subgraphs remains consistent and is normalized within each iteration. We demonstrate the effectiveness of iterative graph normalization at achieving stable normalization outcomes, even for graphs characterized by high tree-width. Furthermore, we show that combining iterative graph normalization with the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem yields state-of-the-art performance in graph data classification tasks. Our findings are supported by experiments involving 14 diverse graph datasets. Importantly, we discover that the traditional method of graph normalization, though performing poorly in certain scenarios, actually excels when dealing with datasets characterized by low tree-width. Consequently, the choice of normalization approach should likely be dataset-dependent. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/FelixEckert/IGNN. Importantly, our label-informed approach is scalable, with the capacity to effectively learn node representations for very large graphs. Notably, under standard evaluation conditions, we discover that LGN outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, with a leading score of 92.35% on the Cora dataset. Specifically, the system CR Draconis consisting of two flare stars is believed to harbor such a plasma source. Our observation findings from 2017 to 2020 show that the CR Draconis plasma source exhibits a distinct 'on-off' behavior tied to the binary's orbital cycle with high-amplitude periodic fluctuations, while also revealing bright low-frequency radiation episodes, even during this 'off' phase. We associate these episodes with transient, strong magnetic activity events. A comprehensive analysis comparing archival optical data with our observational data and modeling the magnetic field structure of CR Draconis allows us to infer the configuration of its magnetic field. We conclude that the CR Draconis plasma source primarily originates from the region around the binary's star-star interaction zone, specifically in the vicinity of white-light radio-emitting regions, and we discuss its potential origins. Moreover, we consider CR Draconis a prototype for studying low-frequency stars in systems with close star-star or star-planet interactions, and it offers unique observational access to the surrounding magnetized plasma via its 'on-off' behavior tied to the binary's orbital cycle. As such, CR Draconis serves as an ideal candidate for long-term observational studies to the meter-class to demonstrate persistent low-frequency emission. Finally, we briefly discuss and compare CR Draconis with other notable objects like HD 159256, Proxima Centauri b, and K2-25b based on their spectral similarity to electron-cyclotron maser emission. Our study presents computational findings on TrCl-Li$_3$ReO$_3$, a trimer-based frustrated quantum magnet, in both planar and two-dimensional arrangements. By utilizing the projective determinant quantum Monte Carlo method, we've extensively explored the ground state properties of TrCl-Li$_3$ReO$_3$, particularly its phase diagram in the presence of a synthetic magnetic field. We've identified several crucial parameters, including the planar spin $S_{\text{eff}}=2.12$ and the inter-trimer exchange $J/J_1=0.12$, which hold significant importance in understanding the characteristics of TrCl-Li$_3$ReO$_3$. Moreover, our observations suggest the existence of multiple phase transitions in the synthetic magnetic field, leading to diverse phase patterns at zero temperature. These phases are largely determined by the ends of ferromagnetic stripes formed by the spins; however, the exact nature of these phases, particularly their natures and relative ratios, exhibits significant variability with the parameters and temperature. u$-model, is proposed to simplify the complex calculations associated with Boltzmann's collision operator in rarefied monatomic gas simulations. By incorporating a dependent collision frequency $
u$, the model aims to incorporate second-order accuracy into the kinetic equation, thereby enabling the incorporation of mean free path terms and higher-order velocity distributions. To optimize the model's performance, the $
u$-model collision frequency is matched with the solution of a modified Boltzmann equation in a boundary layer region, resulting in a usable model for a wide range of Knudsen numbers. The model's applicability is validated through its successful simulation of slippage, thermal slip, and momentum accommodation in simple gas flows. Additionally, the model's properties are evaluated in detailed numerical analysis, and its utility is further illustrated through its application in complex microfluidic and duct flow simulations. Notably, the model successfully predicts the influence of intermolecular potentials on velocity distributions and temperature profiles in carboxylated carbon nanotube pipe flow, thereby refining the accuracy of thermal conditions in nanoscale pipe flow. Natural Language Processing advances have been predominantly in high-tech settings, hampering progress in more down-to-earth settings and hindering AI's real-life application in the courtroom. To bring meaning to AI, researchers are focusing on interpreters that interpret the meaning of unseen text based on prior knowledge and context. Currently, interpreter systems rely on substantial datasets, but extracting human-like meaning from text may not necessarily require a lot of data. We've taken an innovative approach to developing a semantic interpreter using prior knowledge and context, and to our surprise, it works with very minimal data. In this study, we've demonstrated that our interpreter can identify word classifications identical to those of humans with only 1% of the typical dataset. We've achieved this using distributional semantic models that leverage context, integrating multiple context sources, and incorporating various practical techniques. Furthermore, our results reveal our interpreter performs equally well as those trained on significantly larger datasets. This breakthrough suggests that future semantic interpreter systems should draw from a wealth of contextual information, even in the absence of extensive text-based training. Ultimately, this could bring about AI's tangible implementation in settings that have thus far proven challenging for computers to grasp. We've additionally made our code available for public use. 

Please note that this work is an expanded version of our previous exploration, presented at the IJCAI 2020 conference. Additional insights and findings have been added, and our code has been made accessible for the first time. 

For related work on natural language understanding with limited data, please refer to our comprehensive review published in the Journal of Artificial Intelligence.

Researchers at Jefferson National Laboratory are developing advanced silicon sensor technologies for the Electron-Ion Collider.  Three sensor types - honeycomb, stripe, and square - are being explored for use in detectors, with particular emphasis on forward detectors, given the high luminosity requirements of the EIC.  Integrating pixel and calorimeter sensors into a single device could enhance data acquisition and refine the understanding of proton structure, as low-momentum electrons can reveal fine details of the individual protons' Parton Distribution Functions.  Such measurements, however, necessitate extremely high precision at electron detection thresholds, which can be achieved with a combined pixel-calorimeter sensor featuring low material and high hit resolution.  A custom designed, 20 mm x 35 mm square sensor is being developed, featuring a sensitive area of 10 mm x 25 mm, with a proposed pixel array measuring 10 pixels x 17 pixels, with a 25 micron pixel size and deep TPC wells to minimize material, despite only covering 50% of the sensor area.  This design aims to prevent electron detection from detector features such as Coulomb shifts and detector material from contaminating measurements, as well as to minimize data loss due to hits outside of operational regions.  Other forward sensor concepts are also being explored, including a 1 degree polar angle, 2 mm thick honeycomb sensor, with eight different combinations of pixel and calorimeter integrated in a single sensor, with comprehensive studies of the sensor's material impacts on single lepton measurement using the Pythia generator.  Based on these findings, scientists can evaluate the most suitable sensor designs, followed by the fabrication of the selected prototypes.  A separate research project is focused on developing a combined pixel-calorimeter sensor for endcap detectors, requiring data sharing and synchronization between the two distinct sensor types, with particular emphasis on matching found in electron detection.  Research includes sensor integration simulations, pattern recognition, and specific attention to single electron detection, leading to a planned demonstration of the sensor's capabilities once prototypes are in production.  Other topics related to detector development for the EIC are also covered, including EIC goals, detector role in nurturing EIC as a user facility, and nuclear physics underlying detector development for the EIC. The problem of estimating a conditional expectation function, given a dataset and a metric, is explored under both general and asymptotic conditions. It is established that kernel-type estimators yield consistent results across a broad range of metric spaces. Key to this conclusion is the establishment of a novel, asymptotic condition, which defines joint consistency for a class of functions. This condition has far-reaching implications, extending to multi-dimensional conditional expectation operators and yielding a convergence rate of n^-1/4. The efficacy of these estimators is further illustrated by the application of empirical operators in the context of reproducing Hilbert spaces, enabling the derivation of rates for regular variation. The obtained results are supplemental to a recent empirical operator approach introduced by Klement et al. in 2020, and are derived in conjunction with reproducing Hilbert spaces, enabling the derivation of rates for regular variation. The provided estimators are universally constructed and robust, and can be safely used in the presence of dependence, as evidenced by the utilization of a covariance and a reproducing kernel. The methods are numerically evaluated and assessed for their practical application, involving the estimation of a multi-dimensional conditional expectation function on the surface of a unit sphere, as illustrated by a real-world application involving climate modeling. The derived theory and methods are original and intended to contribute to the existing body of knowledge in the field of functional and semi-parametric statistics. The provided code is publicly available on GitHub, and is intended to promote reproducibility and ease of use. Research on Kerr-lens mode-locking has gained significant interest in high-power fiber and crystalline lasers due to its simplicity and broad spectral properties. For solid-state lasers, the phenomenon is characterized by intricate dynamics influenced by multi-dimensional nonlinear coupling, varying Kerr coefficients, and anisotropies in the crystal structure. Although current theories fail to fully account for these complexities, they have led to considerable progress in the field. In contrast, practical applications have often prioritized performance over thorough understanding, especially in recentbreed high-power frequency converters. The ISGMR in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si was studied using inelastic alpha-particle scattering at energies below the ISGMR, with experimental data obtained via the shifting-peak method. In both cases, the ISGMR frequency was observed to decrease with increasing neutron excess. A theoretical model of the ISGMR was developed, assuming independent particle motion and a Steppenbeck's constraint. When the ISGMR and a $0^+$ quadrupole state, which is known to couple strongly with the ISGMR, are considered in the calculation, their experimental evolution is accurately reproduced. This suggests a significant role for coupling between the ISGMR and the $0^+$ quadrupole state in determining their observed behavior. Furthermore, the dependence of the ISGMR frequency on neutron excess can be explained by the effects of both particle density and the $0^+$ quadrupole state's strength. By including the $0^+$ quadrupole state's effect, the predicted ISGMR frequency would exhibit substantially less dependence on neutron excess. The underlying mechanisms of collective phenomena in complex systems are often overlooked, with these systems frequently being characterized by inherent symmetry and pattern regularity. However, collective behaviors can also be triggered by distinct starting conditions, giving rise to diverse, intricate patterns lacking obvious underlying symmetries. By uncovering the hidden symmetrical characteristics of these complex patterns, a novel approach is developed to detect these symmetries directly from the patterns themselves, without reference to any pre-existing symmetry frameworks. An adapted version of the topological model originally proposed by Rosvall and Axelsson is utilized for this purpose. Consequently, this method is demonstrated to effectively identify the underlying topological models in various example systems characterized by intricate, unsymmetrical patterns. Example systems include bird flocks, the dynamics of arrays of Kapitze plates, and temporal patterns in humans and chimpanzees during speech production. Furthermore, this method is shown to be applicable in two main approaches - one in which the underlying topological model is determined directly from the detected clusters, and another in which the detected clusters are first normalized through a reference system. Importantly, the underlying topological models detected in these example systems are found to be consistent with the observed behavioral patterns and are supported by separate observations in existing research. Consequently, the combined results of these approaches offer novel insights into the underlying causes of collective phenomena. Furthermore, the underlying topological models detected in these example systems are found to be consistent with the observed behavioral patterns and are substantiated by separate observations in existing research. Consequently, the combined results of these approaches offer valuable theoretical and practical implications for the analysis of collective phenomena. For instance, the underlying topological models detected in bird flocks, Kapitze plates, and speech production in humans and chimpanzees are found to be consistent with the observed flocking behavior in starling flocks, the wavy patterns produced by Kapitze plates, and the temporal patterns observed in speech production from human and chimpanzee datasets. The detection of topological models through this approach is found to provide key insights into the underlying causes of collective phenomena and to offer valuable suggestions for the analysis of collective behaviors. The present work is found to be separable into two main parts - the derivation of topological models and the interpretation of detected models. Consequently, the underlying causes of collective phenomena and the analysis of collective behaviors are found to be integrally interconnected and influenced by the underlying patterns of activity. The present findings offer a significant breakthrough and inspire further research in the practical application of topological modeling in the analysis of collective behaviors.

The proliferation of geotagged social media data on the web offers considerable potential for understanding human dynamics in public spaces. However, capturing the diverse nature of social media users' movements necessitates extensive data collection covering a broad range of tags across space and time. Existing valuations of social media data in urban settings are typically restricted by the scarcity of data, the high cost of annotation, or the undependable accuracy of existing automatic methods. We propose a voting-based technique for automatic tag validation, which leverages the collective knowledge of multiple supervised learning models. By improving upon existing methods, our approach enhances accuracy and produces diverse tag movements, thereby promoting a deeper comprehension of urban park visitor patterns. Utilizing this method on a large dataset revealed the movements of thousands of visitors in an urban park over an extended period, revealing a diverse set of recurring patterns. We demonstrate the significance of these findings through their relevance to park management and the various nature of social media users' movements. The developed model, known as VALUE, is presented as a feasible solution for the difficult task of tagging in urban environments. Furthermore, we provide insight into the different types of movements by highlighting the distinct characteristics of individuals who frequent the park, employing techniques such as topic modeling. A comprehensive R-related code for VALUE has been made available on our GitHub repository at: https://github.com/m-ahmed7/VLUE.git. Although our primary area of study is urban parks, our proposed model can be applied to a broad array of locations to reveal the underlying social media user movements. We anticipate that the VALUE model will greatly influence various fields of research, and our model can be used as a benchmark for evaluating the efficacy of automated tagging methods in the future. Furthermore, we intend for the developed model to facilitate future studies on understanding human dynamics in the city. Lastly, the developed model aims to enhance the estimation of diverse, unexplored parameters of urban movement distribution curves. A related demonstration is available at: https://demos.cs.umd.edu/demos/voting-based-tag-validation.

We create a new deep learning framework, called NuSPAN, to estimate sparse wavefields in seismic reflection inversion. Existing sparse models are inadequate because their non-uniform sparse wavefield estimates often fail to meet the reflection pattern constraints. NuSPAN overcomes this limitation by integrating a conventional sparse model with a series of convolutional layers. A proximal average network enforces non-ununiform sparsity through structured reflections, while its convolutional layers enhance the estimate's accuracy. We combine NuSPAN with a conjugate gradient method and demonstrate its superiority to SPGAN and CG through both numerical and seismic data tests. Using the Interpretable Seismic Data, for example, NuSPAN surpasses the performance of SPGAN and CG in estimating non-uniform sparse wavefields by 25.6% and 30.1%, respectively. Furthermore, the integration of NuSPAN and conjugate gradient method results in a 52% improvement in inversion convergence compared to the integration of SPGAN and conjugate gradient method. In addition, the estimated sparse wavefields from NuSPAN show a 69% higher truthfulness than those of SPGAN, which the estimated wavefields from CG are the least among the three methods. Lastly, a real seismic-section demonstration illustrates that NuSPAN outperforms the other methods in estimating sparse seismic data with complex non-uniform patterns. All experiments are conducted at ten-fold scales for real seismic-sections. The estimated sparse wavefields from NuSPAN reveal a 77.42% level of truthfulness. Moreover, the other three methods, SPGAN, CG, and their combination, achieve a truthfulness of 8.15%, 4.08%, and 3.55%, respectively. Consequently, NuSPAN shows the potential to enhance the accuracy and convergence of sparse wavefield estimates in seismic reflection inversion. In addition, its expected outcomes can facilitate seismic data interpretation and pattern recognition. Ultimately, the integration of NuSPAN and the conjugate gradient method may lead to the best performance in seismic reflection inversion. Automated part-of-speech (POS) tagging for ancient languages with limited linguistic research can be particularly difficult. Working on texts from 16th century French, we faced such challenges in the {\tt CORSALES} project, where we aim to analyze the literary output of the 16th century's greatest French writers. In this context, we introduce a novel machine learning technique for POS tagging that naturally accommodates ambiguous words, taking into account their etymological and semantic references as found in dictionaries. The proposed algorithm Set-VALP is an adaptation of VALP, a validated processor for the classification of sets-valued attributes, and specifically designed for POS tagging applications. Set-VALP's first stage involves a pre-processing step that identifies potentially ambiguous words, and in a second stage, it submits these words to a machine learning model for re-classification. We evaluate the efficacy of Set-VALP on datasets from the literary output of 16th century French writers, demonstrating its superior performance in comparison to the conventional approach. Furthermore, using a robust computation method, we investigate the properties of the models developed for the two approaches and highlight the distinct role of VALP as a versatile classification tool. This research expands the abstract Riemann integrability, previously defined with real-valued functions, to cover functions with complex values. We theorize that this extension maintains the integrability properties of real-valued functions. Furthermore, the study explores non-continuous Riemann integrability, establishing a connection with a newly introduced concept, weak discontinuity, which divides function sets into continuous and non-continuous elements. We establish that both classes converge to the same limit. The investigation also introduces novel conditions for non-continuous integrability and derives the first derivative from them. The model has potential to apply to functions with complex values in statistical physics, providing novel insights. We demonstrate the applicability to systems characterized by periodic or symmetric indices, such as in the cases of Planar Poincaré maps in 3D dark matter simulations and Poincaré redshift catastrophe in 3D dark matter simulations. The theory is illustrated with a concrete example, the function $f_3(x,y)=1/(xy)+1/\sqrt{x}$. Despite its complex nature, $f_3$ is non-continuously Riemann integrable and the lower and upper Riemann integrals coincide. Moreover, the study shows that both the partial derivatives of $f_3$ and its first derivative are discontinuous. We present a generalized version of $f_3$, enabling the creation of infinite sets of functions with similar properties. The study concludes by comparing our theory with the existing approach to Riemann integrability, previously defined with real-valued functions, and highlights the distinct differences between them. While both are applicable to real-valued functions, only our theory can be extended to functions with complex values. We also address a seemingly unrelated problem, the high number of collisions in the three-body problem, by applying our theory to derive a novel condition for non-continuous integrability. The approach provides a deeper understanding of molecular scattering. According to our model, the scattering of CO and N2 molecules would result in a finite, non-continuous integral. Moreover, the study shows that both the partial derivatives of the integral of $f_3(x,y)$ with respect to $x$ and $y$ are discontinuous. We believe that this unusual behavior may be a hallmark of all Riemann integrable functions with complex values. The study also offers a new method for evaluating the first and second electric multipoles of molecules with complex monopole moments. The method has potential to apply to a wide range of chemical and medical disciplines

Numerical solutions obtained using inverse problem methods are often susceptible to errors due to noisy observational data or the finite precision of computational tools. This research develops a approach to rectify such errors within the context of operator difference equations driven by discrete maps with periodic coefficients. By applying smoothing techniques inspired by heat diffusion and leveraging the properties of the resulting fundamental kernel, our approach enables the construction of a near-optimal operator that minimizes the influence of perturbations. The method is then demonstrated to work by first developing a means to construct a smoothing operator based on the properties of the Green's function for the heat equation on a manifold. Subsequently, we show that the method is equally applicable to operator difference equations and parametric initial value problems driven by discrete-time periodic maps with vector-valued parameters. The method is evaluated using various examples tailored to showcase its applications in various disciplines such as dynamical systems, perturbed differential equations, multidimensional laminates, and the Koopman operator. Furthermore, future directions involving the interplay between manifold learning and our approach are discussed. The research was conducted with support from the CRC 1173 'Optimisation and Rational Models in Energy Systems' and with the assistance of G. V. Sozaei. The method's efficacy was benchmarked using advanced examples requiring significant computational resources, which were generated using the \emph{QuadTruePositve} package, a novel positve-weight pseudorandom number generator designed to reduce noise and accelerate computations. The research was completed with the assistance of S. A. Werder at the University of Freiburg. The smoothening methods developed in this research are now publicly available within the \emph{QuadTruePositve} package. The graphical results were produced using \emph{Matplotlib} and visualized in a \emph{Jupyter} notebook, which is available at: https://jupyter-notebooks.uni-paderborn.de.cnoddev/. G. V. Computing the suspension spectra of these cells as well as their tensor products with other spectra, such as the sphere spectrum and projective spaces, aids in understanding their fundamental group-like behavior. Furthermore, our analysis resolves a question posed by Teichner. Additionally, our results bear resemblance to findings from a separate paper, where the underlying field is replaced with a complete discrete metric space, such as the rational numbers or integers modulo 2. This approach offers a potential method for studying spectra based on other complete discrete metric spaces, such as the additive group of integers modulo some prime number p. Nevertheless, our direct analysis of the quaternionic Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra provides only limited information about their homotopy groups. Hence, we do not the homotopy groups of the direct sum of the spectra based on the additive group of integers modulo 2 and the sphere spectrum be finite. Moreover, our results do not enable us to determine the number of extensions involving these spectra. Thus, further work is necessary to fully comprehend the homotopy groups of these spectra. On a separate note, we offer an alternate proof of a fundamental concept as a means to establish that certain maps, such as those from the sphere to the sphere with one point identified with the south pole, are not split surjections. This new proof relies on the use of free modules. Conversely, the fundamental concept that the module generated by any element is always free is challenged by the existence of the Z/p* Z module, where p* is 2 or some prime number greater than 3. In this case, the dual module is not free. On a related note, we describe a potential approach for determining whether a module is a flat module over some other module by applying the concept that the dual of a locally free module is itself free. This is challenged, however, by the existence of the dual of the Z/p* Z module, where the dual is not locally free. Moreover, our results can be used to construct perfect complexes that are not isomorphic to free modules. In a separate part, our results can be used to construct perfect complexes that are isomorphic to the dual of some other complex, where the complex is itself not locally free. In a related matter, we describe a perfect complex and state that the universal map from some other complex to this one is not a split surjection

Despite research-based advancements being widely available, bringing these into clinical practice has been hindered by issues surrounding data standardization.  Currently, numerous different file formats and encoding methods are being used, which has resulted in data scatter across various platforms. We present a boundary action consistent with Noether's theorem on a pseudo-Riemann surface, and use it to identify a Virasoro algebra on a torus from Noether currents associated with continuous symmetries. It is demonstrated that the central extension in the algebra comes from a variation of the surface's boundary area. Additionally, we show that the surface's entropy is connected to the level number of the Virasoro algebra. When applied to a standard torus, the result yields a value for the entropy that equals the given area. Furthermore, we extend the approach to more general surfaces bounded by multiple loops. The approach can be seen as a field theory interpretation of Bousso's formula, and an analogous statistical mechanics explanation of the result can be formulated. The unification of gravity and Yang-Mills theories may lead to a deeper understanding of the statistical explanation of the entropy. As an aside, the fact that Einstein's general relativity can be expressed in terms of a variational derivative of the Einstein-Hilbert action suggests considering general relativity as a theory of symmetric fields. This idea is in line with the concept of Yang-Mills theory as a theory of gauge fields. The entropy expression also matches Minkowski spacetime's Hilbert challenge. The main findings of the approach have been complemented by a series of graphics that help in understanding the content. The source code for the graphics has been included in the electronic supplement to the paper. The paper began life as a presentation at Charles University in Prague in 2019. The exponentially growing human genome data necessitates novel, efficient, and intelligent analysis techniques to derive meaningful insights. To address the limitations of conventional feature-based approaches, we introduce an unsupervised method that extracts comparable representations from raw genomic data using an autoencoder. By automatically selecting crucial characteristics through sparse encoding, this method enables comparable representations to be learned from diverse genomic sequences, including varying lengths. We successfully demonstrate the applicability of our method to a fundamental genomic analysis task - identifying the closest genomic sequences for a given query using nearest neighbor search. On average, our method with linear models achieves a 25% improvement in classification accuracy over existing feature-based approaches. With the advent of advanced neural network techniques, like transformers, even better representations and performance are likely to be achieved in the future. We also release our method as an open-source, unsupervised, deep learning approach, capable of extracting comparable representations from diverse sequential data, not just genomic data. We anticipate its widespread applications to various areas of computational biology. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/camntassali/seqDNAm.

The behavior of vanadium oxide films, specifically those with a surface structure of (0001), was studied in the context of being in contact with specific metals: hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen. Scanning tunneling microscopy revealed that all these metals cause changes to the films' surface arrangement, leading to a variation in their electrical properties as observed through conductive atomic force microscopy. Specifically, those films treated with hydrogen displayed no signs of a insulating phase, while those treated with carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen exhibited clear indications of a phyllin-like insulating state. However, films treated with oxygen ultimately showed signs of a conduction phase again after being exposed to higher doses. This study highlights the influence of interfacial interactions on controlling the electrical properties of materials. Moreover, those films treated with carbon exhibited a marked resemblance to high-Tc superconductors when analyzed through their power spectra. Moreover, those films treated with nitrogen displayed an unusual dependence of their insulating behavior on bias voltage. This research was conducted at low temperatures, namely 1.5 K. Through utilizing combined techniques of surface science and electronic transport, this study demonstrates that ultra-thin films hold considerable promise in the field of quantum electronics due to their enhanced surface-to-volume ratios compared to their bulk counterparts. Moreover, those films treated with carbon exhibited current cycles dependent on bias voltage that closely resemble those of conventional metallic films. Moreover, those films treated with nitrogen exhibited rectifying properties similar to those of p-n junctions. A new, systematic method (the Clebsch canonization) has been developed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent, canonical Hamiltonian equations. This method provides a clear, algorithmic process for determining canonical representations of Lie-Poisson structures. As a key advantage, it offers a straightforward way to compute Casimirs and their relationships with conserved quantities. As a key challenge, it requires precise control over Poisson transformations and their effects on symplectic structures. Key applications include the conversion of Lie-Poisson structures over various algebraic structures and the representation of the Korteweg-de Vries, nonlinear Schrödinger, and Mikhlin equations. Moreover, it has been shown that Lie-Poisson structures can effectively capture physical characteristics of conservative and dissipative systems, leading to valuable insights into their dynamics. Following the introduction of the canonization procedure, several theoretical results will be proved to illustrate its power and versatility. Lastly, some promising practical examples will be presented, showcasing its utility in practical, engineering settings. The accompanying text can be accessed at a specific URL. The relevant Mathematica code is available for download at another URL. Both are referenced in the text. The method is currently compatible with Lie algebras, Lie groups, and specific, soliton-related equations. Its extension to more complex vector fields and Hamiltonian chains remains an open question. The accompanying code does not currently handle hierarchies of soliton equations, a task left for future development. The provided references cover the relevant literature up to 2021, although the method itself was developed between 2021 and 2022. The associated GitHub repository can be accessed at https://github.com/MaesMark/Clebsch-canonicalization- Lie-Poisson. In our initial study, a general method was presented to derive extensive variables (total mass, momentum, and energy) conservation equations from Euler's equations for an incompressible Navier-Stokes equation system. This paper expands upon that research by applying the method to a compressible Navier-Stokes equation model. The total mass and momentum conservation equations were formulated using the Euler equations for a compressible fluid. The total energy conservation equation was also developed, but unlike in our prior work, due to the compressibility of the fluid, the common factor of density in the kinetic and potential energy was separately derived. A key benefit of our approach is that it conserves the properties of the conservation laws without any additional assumptions. The method's applicability is limited to fluids with constant viscosity and heat transfer properties. A more general method, described in a companion paper, discusses the application of dissipation properties to derive the total energy conservation equation. All three conservation equations were applied to a one-dimensional shock wave example for verification. The results show that the derived conservation equations encompass not only incompressible but also compressible fluid systems. Additionally, the method successfully accounts for both solid boundaries and external forces within the fluid. The total mass and momentum conservation equations are identical to those from Euler's equations, but, unlike the total energy conservation equation, the common factor of density in the kinetic and potential energy requires separate consideration in the compressible fluid system. The total energy conservation equation obtained in this paper is more general and applicable to a wider range of fluids, including both solid boundaries and external forces. Importantly, the method does not rely on assumptions of incompressibility or irrotationality in its application. Consequently, the results indicate that the method is versatile and broadly applicable to a wide range of fluid dynamics systems. The method is particularly effective for deriving conservation equations for systems that previously generated complications, as seen in the examples in our studies. Specifically, the method has the potential to be a powerful tool for further research in fluid dynamics if properly applied. Furthermore, the method may also be applicable to other areas of physics as well, not just fluid dynamics. With minor adjustments, the method could be used for research in other fields as well. Moreover, the method could also be used as a teaching tool to explain and derive various types of fluid dynamics and electromagnetism conservation equations. As an example, Euler's equations for incompressible fluid are discussed in our prior research, while Euler's equations for compressible fluid are discussed in this paper. Accurately predicting non-performing loans is vital for banks, enabling them to make informed decisions when providing credit. We compare the effectiveness of Shallow Neural Networks, Deep Neural Networks, Long Short Time Memory, and Gradient Boosting machines using data from a South East European country to predict non-performing loans. Our best-performing model, a Shallow Neural Network with polynomial regression, achieved a 21.6% error rate and 80% accuracy on the testing dataset, surpassing previous studies. Through feature selection analysis, we identified key variables influencing non-performing loans within this specific region. Our findings highlight the superiority of Shallow Neural Networks in predicting non-performing loans. Moreover, our selection process simplifies the feature selection process and underscores the importance of certain variables. As such, this paper can serve as a starting point for future studies, offering a more controlled and replicable environment for testing different machine learning algorithms and evaluating their performance on different datasets, including financial information on companies. We introduce the Direction Convolutional Network (DRCN), which is designed to process image data in a more informative manner by considering the direction of neighboring pixels for each pixel within an image. The underlying premise is that nearby pixels often have relative directions and orientations, which can provide crucial clues for classification in various scenarios. To achieve this, our DRCN structure incorporates a series of directional convolutional layers comprising a $9\times 9$ kernel with a $7\times 7$ padding arrangement. This unique structure enables the network to explicitly consider the relative directions and orientations of neighboring pixels for each pixel during image classification. Notably, our DRCN framework can be considered a special case of traditional Convolutional Neural Networks with a simplified structure. To validate the efficacy of our approach, we conducted comprehensive experiments with modern image classification datasets, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet, and Small-ImageNet. The results demonstrate that our DRCN framework offers notable advantages over other comparable models. Moreover, our findings suggest that introducing directional components can enhance model generalization, which is a crucial factor for practical applications. Ultimately, our DRCN framework with its unique structural properties has the potential to serve as a pioneering model for image classification tasks across diverse directions. The implementation details and dataset resources for our DRCN framework can be found at the repository link https://github.com/huoyigan2011/DRCN. Furthermore, the technique was adapted to calculate the Zeta function, which is essential for determining the mixed dimension matrix elements of local operators. These matrix elements are essential for various processes, including B to VVL and B to VLD. A novel metric called space utilization has been defined to evaluate how effectively space infrastructure meets the needs of users within a specified region over time, taking into account the temporal distribution of user demands and available resources. This measure assesses the proportion of demands that can be fulfilled under given conditions. This paper applies the space utilization metric to model load factors of ground stations, ship-borne antennas, and low-Earth orbit satellites, showcasing its utility in identifying underutilized or overcrowded infrastructure and optimal deployment strategies for satellites. By leveraging this metric, industry stakeholders can make more informed decisions when investing in new infrastructure and adjusting existing capacity. Furthermore, this concept has broader implications for research and development in the space industry, extending to other types of orbital systems. Several applications of the space utilization metric have been presented at conferences and published in journals, leading to various uses such as: optimizing satellite constellations for ship-based antennas, suggesting strategies for balancing ground station load factors, and using the concept in machine learning applications for predicting transponder occupancy. The research was initially published in a technical report in 2021 and has since been applied in multiple scenarios. One potential limitation of the space utilization metric is its assumption of simultaneous transactions, which may not accurately represent non-real-time applications, prompting further research on relaxing this assumption. Additionally, future studies could explore various applications, such as identifying overcrowding in the system, influencing deployment strategies, introducing selective capacity allocation, and expanding the definition of the space utilization metric. Several potential extensions of the space utilization metric have been proposed, but the optimization of two-dimensional ground stations with constraints remains an area for further research. Moreover, the space utilization concept has been utilized in other orbital systems such as satellite constellations and gravitational Assist Orbit Utilization Systems. Finally, the space utilization metric has been employed in non-orbital settings like wireless sensor networks, demonstrating its broader applicability and relevance to connectivity-focused infrastructure. The concept of space utilization has been influential in research, with several studies building upon it and numerous results being presented at conferences and published in journals, leading to the achievement of the best paper award at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Communications and Analytics. With ongoing work still anticipated, the space utilization metric continues to inspire research and applications. With regards to completeness, it is worth noting a recent publication titled "Fundamental Limits of Passive Satellite Communications: Optimizing Code Selection and Physical-Layer Networks" that presents related yet distinct concepts. Moreover, the space utilization concept has been recently applied in the context of Internet of Underwater Things.

Literature serves as a vital source of knowledge and language inspiration. Though conventional methods like text summarization and generation can utilize language patterns from books, they may not accurately capture the intricate spirit and intent behind a story. To deeply analyze and understand literature, we developed the LitMind Lexicon, a comprehensive dictionary that enables users to explore literary devices, symbols, and other thematic elements within Chinese modern and contemporary novels. This dictionary not only facilitates in-depth literary studies but also serves as a valuable resource for AI-powered content creation and education. Our research presents the underlying design of the LitMind Lexicon, its constructed methodologies, and the potential applications and implications of this innovative tool. Our findings demonstrate that the LitMind Lexicon exceeds existing literature databases and can be accessed online through a secure HTTPS connection. A detailed user guide and technical manual are available for reference. The data collection, dictionary development, source code, and online platform can be accessed at the provided websites. The LitMind Lexicon aims to promote literature research, cultivate linguistic awareness, and foster a greater appreciation for reading and writing. To date, our dictionary covers 115 novels, 15,369 terms, and 215,951 sentence examples. Our novel data sets, built from real-world data, have helped inform various AI applications, shedding new light on how AIs comprehend literature. Our results indicate that the LitMind Lexicon has yielded substantial literature research outcomes, as evidenced by our 11 prominent publications in leading conferences and journals. The online platform and user community have attracted the attention of over 1,000 registered users, driving the development and evolution of the dictionary. Our work highlights the tremendous potential of the LitMind Lexicon to revolutionize literature research, and we anticipate it to continue inspiring future research and applications. As of December 2023, our dictionary covers 165 novels, 18,719 terms, and 281,664 sentence examples. In this updated version, we have incorporated various novel data sets, including 35 works of Classical Chinese Novels, 17 collections of Classical Chinese Poetry, and 15 Encyclopedia of Myths and Legends. In the future, we intend to enrich the LitMind Lexicon with more content from diverse literature genres and explore the integration of the dictionary with other AI technologies to push the boundaries of literature research and content creation. The continued growth of the LitMind Lexicon will depend on user contributions, and we look forward to seeing what other researchers and community members can achieve with this innovative tool. In contexts where classes aren't perfectly balanced, near neighbors classification has an essential function yet the technique's performance is hindered when dealing with highly unbalanced datasets and noisy data due to over-emphasis on distant cases. This study presents an approach to near neighbors classification that disperses cases in a balanced manner by utilizing a selective set of nearest neighbors. The method involves weighting distances to maintain a balanced ratio of positive and negative cases and incorporates a robust metric for noisy data. A comprehensive simulation is conducted to assess the efficacy and stability of this approach. The algorithm is also applied to real-world datasets, specifically a set of patient records that experienced irregularities due to the influence of powerful medical devices, and demonstrates significant improvement over established methods. The proposed algorithm is further made accessible in R for easy implementation. As this problem falls under complex intrinsically imbalanced scenarios, the suggested methodology isn't solely confined to this type of problem but may be more broadly applicable. Recently, researchers introduced the concept of entropic discontinuities for nonlinear hyperbolic systems, a more inclusive category than shock waves. Although entropic discontinuities have contractive properties similar to those of rarefaction curves, the standard contraction arguments are only applicable to precursors of standard rarefaction waves and require initial data to lie within a specified interval. To overcome this limitation, researchers have been working on developing more flexible and relevant contraction arguments for use in theoretical analysis and numerical standardization of entropic discontinuities. In this paper, we review and refine the existing theory and provide new insights into entropic discontinuities for weakly nonlinear hyperbolic systems. Our goal is to create a theoretical framework for numerical standardization of entropic discontinuities via finite volume and flux difference matrices. In particular, we demonstrate the potential advantages of using first-order and central difference schemes in conjunction with entropic difference matrices to preserve the entropy condition for more diverse initial data sets, including those that may not fall within the typical range for standard rarefaction waves. Furthermore, we extend the theory to include conservation laws with non-conservative terms, a class of problems known as reduction-type equations, and we illustrate our results with numerical examples. We also specify conditions under which the entropic difference matrices remain positive, even in cases involving complex systems of conservation laws. In addition to its theoretical contributions, this paper showcases the applications of entropic difference matrices for use in conserving intensive variables and reducing variance in numerical simulations. In particular, we demonstrate its potential for use in modeling complex phenomena, including the interaction between fluid and free surface flows, where the use of entropic difference matrices helps to reduce numerical oscillations. In summary, we extend the theory of entropic difference matrices for use in numerical standardization of entropic discontinuities, including cases involving non-conservative terms, introduce new applications of entropic difference matrices, and illustrate its relevance to diverse problems in partial differential equations and their associated numerical simulations. Through numerical examples and results, we demonstrate the potential of entropic difference matrices in improving standardization in various contexts and the researcher anticipates further developments in this area. In particular, future work could involve using entropic difference matrices for approximating solutions of nonlinear hyperbolic systems, a task made more pressing due to the lack of accurate solution methods for such problems. In particular, entropic difference matrices show much potential in modeling reduction-type equations, a task made more pressing due to the recent experiments that demonstrate the relevance of reduction-type equations in various applications. We investigate the temporal stability in a metric space context for the Hunter-Saxton PDE, focusing on solutions that exhibit Lipschitz continuity. We prove that these solutions are well-defined, and their temporal stability within a specified metric space is established, with the distance function being directly proportional to the $L^2$ norm of their evolution over time. Additionally, by leveraging this stability result, the relationship between the Lipschitz continuity of the solution is linked to the existence of a curve with minimal variation. This curve's existence is connected to the $L^2$ norm of the solution's time-evolution through the application of a Prodi-Perelis type theorem. Concluding our findings, a relationship between the measures of solution continuity and its spatial regularity is determined. Key aspects of this work include being entirely based on properties of the Hunter-Saxton equation itself, and employing novel mathematical approaches that were recently established in a study by J. M. Ballard and the author. Furthermore, the methods utilized are largely independent of the function form, allowing them to be adapted and applied to a broader range of partial differential equations. Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging can be beneficial during spinal surgery, but high dependability and consistency are necessary for reliable clinical decision-making. We compared robotic scanning, performed by paraoperative staff members, with traditional manual scanning for accuracy in detecting spinal curvature. The study revealed that robotic scanning, using the ULTRACAM system, yielded consistent results and showed a high correlation with manual scanning. Specifically, we found that robotic scanning produced consistent measurements with coefficients of variation (CVs) below 9% for different curvatures, while also accurately localizing key spinal structures within 5 mm. In comparison, manual scanning achieved a maximum CV of 13% across various curves. Notably, there was no significant difference between the two techniques in terms of lumbar curve corrections. We concluded that robotic scanning, used in conjunction with ULTRACAM, produces reliable and repeatable measurements for scoliosis assessment, demonstrating its potential as a trustworthy tool in both research and clinical settings. The results suggest that robotic scanning could be applied to various orthopedic assessments, such as verifying implant positioning after spinal surgery. Moreover, ULTRACAM's capacity for automatic spinal detection, shape calculation, and marker tracking could facilitate accelerated and user-friendly scoliosis evaluations, ultimately facilitating paraoperative decision-making. Such a system could also support the development of image-guided scintigraphy to optimize scoliosis treatment. Contrary to traditional inflection point-based methods, our approach models the natural variability of speech through a sequence of medians. We separate speech into manageable segments around these medians and optimize the acoustic characteristics within each partition. We have successfully tested this method in several scenarios, including untrained median optimization, cross-speaker duration prediction, and limited data speaker adaptation. Our results demonstrate substantial improvements in subjective quality ratings as well as lower Mean Absolute Error compared to a widely used TACOTUVA-based method.
