Nonetheless, the duplicate nature of their architecture leads to inefficient sharing of features, which hinders their performance. In an effort to optimize this efficiency, researchers have latestly turned to rearranging the channels within their sub-networks via random permutation. This paper seeks to enhance the effectiveness of MIMO architecture through a different approach. By merging specific primary convolutional layers into primary blocks and assigning these blocks across the network in a uniform manner, we can enhance the sharing of primary features. Moreover, we can fine-tune the allocation of primary blocks and hidden convolutional layers to ensure that the data dimension remains compatible and the network's capacity is adequately provided. This novel method, dubbed Structured Shuffle, yields superior performance and reduced parameters across a variety of tasks. Notably, our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art performance in semantic segmentation and image denoising. Furthermore, our method significantly reduces the parameters and activations in image recognition and semantic segmentation tasks. Moreover, we extend the application of our method to video recognition and compression and achieve state-of-the-art results in these fields. This research presents a comprehensive examination of existing datasets containing images of historical manuscripts. Typically, such datasets cater to specific requirements of machine learning and deep learning models, which often necessitate the distinction between individual characters and compound symbols. Consequently, many datasets have been developed with a focus on categorizing characters, while others prioritize identifying enclosed entities. Despite these varied research approaches, there is no standardized collection of existing datasets in the field, hindering comparative studies and limiting the exchange of ideas. To bridge this gap, this survey collects and consolidates information on existing datasets in a unified structure, with the aim of presenting their characteristics in a concise and accessible format. Furthermore, relevant papers that utilize these datasets for training machine learning and deep learning models are included in the survey, offering insights into the research objectives and outcomes. Ultimately, this academic contribution is intended to enhance understanding of this subject among researchers and scientists, while sparking innovative discussions and collaborations that can advance the development of computational methods for analyzing historical manuscripts, ultimately driving more effective research in the field. High-performance robotic systems require precise position and velocity control. However, conventional methods used for controlling industrial robots fall short in achieving such control due to limitations in their design. This research presents an innovative approach to enhance the position and velocity control capabilities of a two-axis robot by incorporating additional sensors. By utilizing "helper sensors" at each joint to measure the acceleration and velocity, the proposed scheme can streamline the processing and integration of position data, thereby improving the overall system's dynamics. In turn, this leads to robust and disturbance-resistant closed-loop dynamics with enhanced smoothness. Notably, the proposed idea is adaptable to various industrial robot designs, making it practically applicable for immediate implementation. Simulation results are provided to demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed solution, and its efficacy will be experimentally validated in an actual robotic setup. Following the derivation of regulations for a general N-axis robotic system, this study specifically demonstrates the application of its findings to a two-axis flexible robotic arm. By incorporating additional position data sources, the proposed scheme successfully enhances the position and velocity tracking capabilities of the two-axis robotic system. Moreover, the introduction of pseudo-inertial mass and pseudo potential in the revised dynamics equations accelerates the closing time of the system and accelerates the system towards the equilibrium state. Furthermore, the proposed idea is tested using a B11 six-axis robotic arm built by ABB to verify its effectiveness in practical applications. The corresponding MATLAB and Simulink files related to this study can be accessed at the provided repository. Recent research on transport within the molecular continuum has primarily focused on individual scattering sites, such as steps, edges, and defects, with less attention devoted to more complex structures like molecules. Although molecular surfaces feature multiple energy minima that significantly impact transport, applying the traditional parameter-free algorithm to this type of problem is impractical. In order to accurately analyze energy patterns and investigate the influence of individual atoms, researchers developed a novel multi-center implementation of the parameter-free algorithm. This innovative method is based on a hexagonal grid consisting of three by three transmission channels, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of energy patterns and general transport principles. Moreover, the developed algorithm can be easily adapted into a highly performing Fortran program. To validate its effectiveness, the new multi-center implementation was applied to a variety of problems, including a flat graphene layer, 6P ring, and pentacene molecule. By doing so, researchers were able to uncover new findings about the physical properties of these systems, such as their transmission patterns, energy-level distributions, and molecular spectra. Importantly, the new multi-center implementation was able to accurately simulate energy patterns and transport data for the 6P ring, while its application to pentacene allowed for the simulation of its red-shifted dipole blockade for the first time. Ultimately, the new multi-center implementation has far-reaching applications and can serve as a valuable computational tool for investigating a wide range of scattering sites and molecular structures in the molecular continuum. First, the problem of determining the metric dimension parameterized by feedback vertex number $k$ is NP-hard, with no approximation algorithm that can determine whether the metric dimension is at most $k + 1$ unless $k$ is zero, except for the scenario where $k$ equals the number of vertices in the graph. Furthermore, for the graph classes $P_n$ and C_n, we are able to either solve the problem exactly or determine upper and lower bounds for the metric dimension, which in turn allows us to derive explicit values for the metric dimension of these graph classes parameterized by the feedback vertex number. This paper delves into the Yang-Mills theories with highest spin symmetries, investigating how these theories relate to self-dual theories through the perspective of twistor operators. By constructing a nonlinear operator that incorporates the interaction of gauge fields, we establish a nonlinear relation between Yang-Mills theories and their self-dual counterparts. This results in a correlation between non-linear twistor equations and the classical Yang-Mills theory, thereby establishing an alternative formulation for its non-linear equations of motion. Moreover, the paper's methods are exemplified in four-dimensional free Yang-Mills theory, as well as in five-dimensional free Yang-Mills theory, which is shown to be equivalent to a complex twistor equation in five dimensions. Finally, the paper draws connections to superymmetric Yang-Mills theories, revealing that twistor operators can be superymmetrized by extending their definition to a superspace description of field theory. A related notion of 'twistors' arises from the supersymmetric extension of the nonlinear twistor equation, emphasizing its distinct nature from the traditional concept of a super-twistors known from superymmetric Yang-Mills theory. A simple application of this notion in five-dimensional free Yang-Mills theory provides an alternative path to deriving the holomorphic Yang-Mills equations through the method of superymmetric Yang-Mills theory. Additionally, the paper's methods are shown to be compatible with non-linear realizations of supersymmetry, a concept to be explored further in future research. One of the research's key outcomes is the demonstration that supersymmetry can be superymmetrized in a superspace description of a theory initially defined through the nonlinear Yang-Mills equations.  Notably, the combined effect of the non-linear twistor equation and supersymmetry, two concepts rooted in algebraic geometry and supersymmetry theory respectively, may ultimately facilitate a comprehensive synthesis of these ideas into a geometric formulation of Yang-Mills theory. Although the question of geometric formulation remains unresolved, one of the research's key claims provides an initial step in this direction by claiming that geometric formulation is, in fact, possible. A related conjecture proposes a correspondence between geometric construction, algebraic properties, and a distinct notion of 'geometric supersymmetry' proposed in the research. Such a geometric supersymmetry notion could potentially serve as a unique bridge between Yang-Mills theory and superymmetric Yang-Mills theory, thereby enabling a distinct geometric interpretation of these theories as the research intends to further explore. The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, current deep learning approaches often struggle with accurate classification when presented with noisy labels. To address this issue, our study introduces an innovative method known as the BGLRM (Bayesian Statistics Guided Label Rejuvenation Model) that utilizes Bayesian statistics to detect and correct noisy labels. BGLRM incorporates two key schemes - the Deep Bayesian Neural Network (DBBNN) and the Label Correction Mechanism (LCM). The DBBNN generates a noise-aware posterior distribution for predicted labels, while the LCM seeks to minimize prediction discrepancies between the model and the learned label posterior distributions. Our comprehensive evaluations, conducted using two datasets contaminated with artificial and real-world noise, demonstrate that BGLRM significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods by a substantial margin. The source code for BGLRM is available on GitHub at https://github.com/simonwang121/SSL4MRI. The Experimental Results are displayed on an online dashboard at https://label-noise-demo.herokuapp.com. Ultimately, our empirical analysis reveals that robust deep neural networks are crucial for accurate domain adaptation in medical image classification. The proposed BGLRM is envisioned to have a range of potential applications in the practical world of medical imaging. To address this problem, we introduced a timed definition package in HOL, which allows a function to be defined differently over time and makes any unapproved definitions invalid. We implemented this idea on the HOL Light platform and demonstrated its benefits through several examples. Additionally, we further modified the definition structure in HOL to include preconditions and further developed the timed definition package to include time-based recursion and multiple timing parameters. We then successfully applied this tool to recreate a timed version of the ARM architecture in HOL, confirming its correctness. Furthermore, we used the tool to improve HOL's existing functions such as div, mod, pow, and map, which were originally incorrectly implemented and caused issues in the arm architecture due to unapproved definitions. To address these errors, we further modified the timed definition package to include explicit type restrictions, resulting in improved performance. To showcase its benefits, we used the tool to speed up ARM calculations by 15% to 67% and explained its impact. We also further modified the definition structure in HOL to incorporate nested timing parameters and recursively defined functions, which greatly benefited complex calculations like Wilson's theorem and the Fibonacci sequence, with performance improvements of 40% and 60% respectively. Finally, we successfully applied the tool to improve HOL's modular arithmetic by rewriting key functions such as div, mod, and pow to be more efficient, which significantly accelerated arm calculations and corrected previous errors, with improvements of 30% to 65%. Key insights from the fundamental dynamics of the phenomenon are extracted from numerical simulations, with the aim of optimizing a model that only considers the critical wall-normal velocity as an input. By integrating empirical data into a theoretical framework, where the dynamics at the finest resolution are assumed to follow a specific simple rules, a significant enhancement of the model's predictive capacity is achieved. Notably, with just one optimizing parameter and no adjustment to the model's core mechanics, the model's accuracy in replicating the wall-pressure spectrum is improved by an order of magnitude, particularly in the relevant frequency range for wall coherent structures. Furthermore, this refinement results in substantial reductions in the computed residual kinetic energy and root-mean-square error when compared to the original model. Moreover, the optimized model is surprisingly accurate in replicating the characteristics of instantaneous flow separation behind wall coherent structures. Consequently, this approach to model refinement can be broadly applied to diverse coherent structure-based models, with implications for the theoretical understanding and computational utilization of wall-bound turbulence as a whole. Moreover, with the advent of machine learning, this process can now be even more seamlessly integrated and data-driven in approach. We investigate the additive anomaly in a Born-Infeld infant Skyrme model and demonstrate that the underlying equations form a classical system possessing three degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we establish the existence of self-dual solutions for this system, revealing a characteristic hyperboloid shape. In the context of the Skyrme model, these self-dual solutions take the form of solitons possessing quark number one. Notably, for the Born-Infeld infant Skyrme model, these solitons exhibit localized magnetic field patterns without associated charge distributions. In contrast, for the standard Skyrme model, such a configuration would result in a non-self dual state. Lastly, we present initial value problems associated with the additive anomaly equation in the Born-Infeld infant Skyrme model and demonstrate the non-existence of smooth, decaying solutions. Consequently, this system is shown to be non-integrable. In conclusion, while the standard Skyrme model supports general hyperboloid shapes as self-dual configurations, the Born-Infeld infant Skyrme model is constrained to this form alone. Additionally, we confirm the non-existence of smooth, decimating solutions for initial value problems associated with the additive anomaly equation in the Born-Infeld infant Skyrme model. Hence, the additive anomaly equation in this model is found to be non-integrable as well. The present study indicates non-local effects inherent to non-Abelian gauge theories can introduce novel, intriguing features to these systems. These non-local effects may lead to the emergence of unusual physics, such as those observed in the examples discussed above, that may require thorough examination. Moreover, they may also facilitate the creation of unique solutions where various physical properties are decoupled. Notably, the additive anomaly itself becomes negligible in well-known Skyrme model configurations with hyperboloid shapes as self-dual solutions. In contrast, for the Born-Infeld infant Skyrme model, these solitons exhibit localized magnetic field patterns without associated charge distributions. Consequently, the total charge decreases, and the magnetic field increases, resulting in the additive anomaly dominating this system. In contrast, for the standard Skyrme model, such a configuration would result in a non-self dual state. Hence, the underlying total charge increases via this process. The evolution of Weyl semimetals under periodic lattices or pseudomagnetic fields leads to complex semi-metal or insulator transitions. Most analyses of these systems ignore time-reversal symmetry, but in reality, this symmetry often plays a significant role. Our study examines the effect of broken time-reversal symmetry in a two-dimensional Weyl semimetal with pseudomagnetic fields applied to one or both spin components. At the benchmark Chern number of 2, we find that each edge of the dispersion curve supports a single Weyl branch moving opposite to the expected direction, with a corresponding opposite moving Weyl branch at the other edge of the dispersion curve. Analytically, we determine the exact momentum dependence around Van Hove singularities, and through diagonalization, we confirm that these behaviors hold even when interactions are considered. Transitions between semi-metal and insulator states in this system exhibit unique characteristics of Larkin-Ovchinnikov, Fulde-Ferari, and up-up-down orders. Additionally, we identify Larkin-Ovchinnikov states and up-up-down domains within specific pseudomagnetic field configurations. Our work also extends to the higher regime of the Hofstadter Chern number, and we offer potential pathways for experimentally verifying time-reversal symmetry in this type of system. Furthermore, our study highlights possible time-reversal symmetry-breaking states with non-zero Berry curvature within nonMagnetically doped Graphene systems. The effective screening of long-range forces plays a significant role in the physical properties of various media. In collective particle systems, including colloids and granular matter, the concept of screening differs from its application in traditional plasma theory. Our research focuses on the mechanical properties of discrete, three-dimensional granular columns under static conditions, where an applied force is generated through the weight difference between a embedded marble and an unembedded one. By experimenting and numerically simulating the stress on both embedded and unembedded particles, we found evidence supporting the anomalous screening model previously proposed. The ANM predicts a shorter screening length relative to standard plasma theory, specifically proportional to $\log(N)/N$ rather than $1/N$. Our findings confirm that the ANM is applicable in the range from $N=5$ to $300$, with experiments and simulations demonstrating consistent ratios of screening lengths in both static and dynamic conditions. Furthermore, we observed a non-random distribution of particles in columns subjected to forces, which correlates with weaker interactions between particles and contrasts typical behavior in colloid systems. Our study provides comprehensive validation of the ANM through both experimental and numerical approaches, paving the way for future investigations of the impact of normal forces on screening phenomena. Ultimately, our research could lead to a deeper understanding of the mechanical properties governing collective discrete systems. The Fast Multipole Method, a widely used technique for speeding up direct N-body simulations in molecular dynamics, preserves total angular momentum in its updated force calculations. This is because when updating forces at a given point, FMM only considers interactions involving that point and those of identical parity (same or opposite charge and spin orientation), and it does so through a straightforward vector calculation without any proxy particle generation. In doing so, the method ensures that any fictitious charges introduced during tree traversal are canceled out, and the update of torques for individual dipoles also preserves angular momentum. As a result, implementing FMM in per-atom codes is relatively straightforward, and the updated source code, along with the corresponding FMM headers, is provided for the HOOMD-Blue framework. We also demonstrate that, contrary to popular belief, both particle and proxy particle approaches yield identical results when properly implemented, and the reasons behind this equivalence are identified. Lastly, incorporating FMM in non-periodic simulation scenarios, such as NVE simulations with no winders, presents an additional challenge that needs to be addressed. Although this issue only affects scenarios with perfectly conserved quantities like angular momentum, it turns out that proxy particles can't accurately reproduce the correct outcome because they inherently introduce artificial symmetry breaking forces, and proxy particles are only beneficial in scenarios where the method's pseudosymmetry is a key advantage. We further explain that proxy particles can't accurately preserve angular momentum because they involve an artificial redistribution of charge over a atom's surface based on its normal vector, which artificially breaks parity symmetry, whereas FMM only uses charge and parity to group relevant interactions together. As a result, the implementation of FMM in MD codes requires an adjustment of the usual proxy particle workflow, and the method's understanding needs to be extended to include the proxy particle approach for symmetric interactions. Following this extension, implementing both the particle and proxy particle approaches of FMM is relatively straightforward within HOOMD-Blue. We further investigate why these two approaches yield identical results when properly implemented and find that, contrary to the expectations based on the current understanding of the FMM algorithm, the particle approach actually appears to be a special case of the proxy particle approach, and the main reason for the correctness of the proxy particle implementation of FMM turns out to be a nearly identical set of equations for proxy particles of identical parity as the ones used in the N-body algorithm. Only a minor additional correction is needed for particles with opposite parity. This further implementation detail requires that proxy particles be implemented for both data and force

Laser development has long presented two major challenges: obtaining precise control over the lasing frequency and maintaining consistent single-longitudinal-mode operation. To address these issues, we implemented a digital method for an external-cavity semiconductor laser to produce a distributed feedback laser with a single longitudinal mode and controlled transition frequencies. Using high-speed modulation of a driver voltage combined with fast feedback loop adjustment, we successfully enabled rapid frequency tuning of the lasing frequency, yielding a fast response of 1 nanosecond. This frequency tuning was carried out at various driving speeds, allowing for the generation of frequency chirps, as well as multi-pulse patterns with frequencies that varied from 1 MHz to 14 GHz, created through electronic modulation of the driver voltage. Furthermore, we observed a digital bandpass filter effect, where the spectrum showed sharp peaks with narrow bases and smooth frequency transitions. We also measured the laser's coherence properties, revealing a relatively narrow spectral line (0.278 kHz at 2.53 GHz) and long-time persistent time (6.gh) due to the digital method of single-mode operation. This digital approach to lasers offers a highly advanced technique for the development of advanced optical clock systems and frequency stabilization. It has the potential to contribute significantly to the construction of precise optical clock systems, as well as broadening the capabilities of lasers in scientific investigations and applications. By examining the changes in urban encounter dynamics, we found that the period with the lowest diversity in encounters coincided with the highest pandemic impact. The pandemic altered urban behavior in two primary ways, causing a shift from homogeneous to more extreme heterogeneous configurations. Initially, the adoption of social distancing policies resulted in a concentration of users within a limited number of zones, promoting more homogeneous encounters. Conversely, the combination of confinement and varied pandemic regulations led to a scattering of users across the city, ultimately increasing the likelihood of encounters with a wide range of participants. By utilizing an information-theoretic measurement, we determined that the average income diversity of urban encounters peaked at around 70% following the introduction of social distancing measures due to an increased variation in user locations. Following this period, the decrease in the likelihood of encounters with a wide range of participants, along with an increased concentration of users at urban edges, ultimately reduced the income diversity of urban encounters. Our findings also highlight a notable age disparity in response to the pandemic, as individuals, particularly those with younger ages, exhibited more homogeneous behavior. Conversely, the increased diversity in encounters among older individuals was due to a combination of their reduced use of the urban infrastructure and adherence to the social distancing guidelines. Our analysis indicates that the primary factor behind the decline in income diversity of urban encounters was a result of fewer multi-age encounters, as the increased diversity among individual groups was not a contributing factor. By employing a complex dynamics model, we demonstrated that the diversity in urban encounters could recover over time. We explore the development of standardized behavior in robots through their interactions with multiple co-operative humans, which have diverse ways of interacting with them. We found that within co-operative human-robot interactions, robots tend to develop predictable, task-related behaviors such as gesturing towards tools or demonstrating how to use them. These predictable patterns present an opportunity for humans to teach robots novel behaviors by leveraging these expectations. We developed a decision-theory-based model that outlines how human instructions are influenced by these predictive patterns and confirmed this through a large-scale experiment with 300 participants. This research contributes to the growth of robot learning and planning standards by providing insights into the nature of robot communication in co-operative human-robot interactions. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that by working alongside various human co-operative agents across different tasks, robots can develop and learn more effective and robust ways to communicate with and interact with humans in the future. By leveraging experimental data from an X-ray flash experiment on polyethylene sheets, we employ a dual-energy CT method that utilizes two energy settings to differentiate between plastic and air. Our approach involves three main steps: initially, we use prior knowledge about the material's density to separate polyethylene from the air, followed by the removal of flaws in the image, and finally, we reweight the image pixels to accurately differentiate between plastic and air using a parameterized model. Electromagnetic gap plasmons are characteristic of subwavelength nanoparticles connected by small gaps. Predicting their properties is complicated by electron spillover and nonlocal effects, which integrate various length scales. To clarify these influences, we investigated a specific case of a nanoscale gap in the range of vanishingly small distances. Within the framework of classical electrodynamics, we found that both nonlocality and electron spillover cause significant frequency shifts, gap dependence, and damping, which suggests these effects should not be neglected in modeling plasmonics of small gaps. To understand nonlocality, we applied different forms of permittivity adjustment and quantum potentials, showing that the particle-size gap relationship and electron behavior are key factors. Our findings provide valuable insights for accurately modeling plasmonics in the rapidly developing field of nanophotonics. Additionally, we established a critical rule of thumb for work gap gaps smaller than 1 nanometer should not be treated as isolated particles. Conversely, gaps larger than 0.5 nanometers can be approximated using the widely used dipole model with reasonable accuracy. This conclusion has significant practical implications for nanophotonics research and application. Lastly, we briefly discuss quantum simulations of the quantum plasmon, which have been ongoing for decades. Future simulation approaches should take into account the quantum potential's significant influence on the quasichemical gap plasmon spectrum, allowing for meaningful comparisons with experimental findings and classical models. Such comparisons could lead to new simulation methods for analyzing near field phenomena. Potentially relevant applications of this sort could be discovered through reverse engineering, which may involve nanoscale quantum cavities, optical nanosensors, superintensity, and splitting light into multiple frequencies. We develop a new theory that takes into consideration the effect of solvent polarization and derive a dimensionless parameter to characterize the degree of solvent polarization. We analyze the conditions under which solvent polarization significantly impacts the surface charge distribution and identify the parameters necessary for maximizing the electric field at the surface. We find that a high degree of surface flexibility does not necessarily lead to a high electric field; instead, we identify specific surface charge and polymer repeat length values that result in the maximum electric field strength. We also investigate how the number and size distribution of ions affect the surface charge distribution and identify monovalent ions with a specific charge as optimal for maximum electric field occurrence. Automated end-to-end processing of unstructured specification documents remains a critical challenge in the field. Despite significant breakthroughs in processing natural language text, the problem persists due to distinctive characteristics of specification documents, such as intricate tables, multi-faceted knowledge, and complex multi-layered structures. In response to this challenge, we developed a novel solution comprising of a document transformation framework and a knowledge graph-based search engine for extracting software specifications. The search engine is fueled by a knowledge graph leavened with diverse data from various sources, such as software manuals, scientific research, and crowd-sourced data. The framework incorporates a hybrid clustering and search algorithm that integrates element similarity with sequence-based hooks. The approach leverages a hybrid search engine for extracting software specifications that combines a tile-based search with a word2vec-powered search. The hybrid search engine is comprised of a tile-based search for rapid table-based search and a word2vec-powered search for in-depth structured knowledge extraction. The hybrid search engine is designed to provide a dual-layered search of specification documents, allowing users to navigate and select specifications based on a combination of semantic and structural hooks. We evaluated our approach by applying it to over 100,000 software packages, extracting more than 18 million software-specific knowledge graph entries across 7856 Public Git Hub repositories, thereby demonstrating its feasibility and scalability. The empirical analysis of the search engine reveals that the majority of users (70%) use the hybrid search engine to navigate and extract software specifications across diverse taxonomic kingdoms, including domain-specific little language, domain-agnostic languages, design languages, knowledge graphs, and ontologies. Furthermore, we observed that the hybrid search engine generates a wealth of implicit and explicit hooks, including semantic, structural, syntax-driven, and hook-driven hooks, thereby shedding light on the narrative structure and user perception of specification search. We also discovered that the hybrid search engine is capable of detecting emergent hooks as users interactively navigate the hybrid search engine, thereby demonstrating its capacity for hook augmentation. The hybrid search engine is capable of reducing search time by 65% in the presence of OEM and AGILE search modes, thereby showcasing its potential for user-centric hybrid search. Ultimately, we empirically analyzed and demonstrated the hybrid search engine's ability to extend the current state-of-the-art software specification search beyond the realm of domain experts, thereby empowering crowdsourced and end-user search. The technique is poised to revolutionize a wide variety of data extraction and search-based tasks across diverse domains, thereby empowering the future of end-user participation in software specification search

In this research, we investigated the adversarial vulnerability of a neural network in modulation classification. We discovered that generating robust results involves creating adversarial samples to improve the model's resistance. To accomplish this task, we utilized an adversarial training method known as adversarial pair generation (APG) and a hybrid generative adversarial model (blend GAN). This model consists of two generative adversarial models, including a standard generative adversarial model and a generative adversarial model with clean data. We applied the blend GAN to the modulation classification task and achieved promising results, showcasing its effectiveness in producing robust samples and enhancing the model's resistance to adversarial attacks. Additionally, under adversarial conditions, the blend GAN exhibited superior performance in maintaining low adversarial error rates and achieving high classification accuracy with input data. Furthermore, we compared the results of the blend GAN with those of traditional generative adversarial methods and adversarial training. We found that the blend GAN outperformed these methods in robustness and classification accuracy. We validated our findings through repeated experiments with data from different sources. The implementation details and code are available online at https://github.com/Maammar/bGAN_MC. We performed an influence assessment to determine the accuracy of our results. The analysis revealed that the parameters significantly influenced the results, whereas other parameters had minimal effects. Specifically, we identified parametric sensitivity and feature redundancy as potential areas for improvement in this research. In order to enhance the model's resistance to adversarial attacks, it is crucial for future works to focus on the parameters with substantial influences, namely, the number of iterations in the blend GAN training and the size of the clean data set. Potentially incorporating noise data into the generative model could also be beneficial. A future work could involve adding noise data to the generative model to observe its effects on the results. Additionally, the effect of robust training techniques on the model's resistance to adversarial attacks is another area that needs to be explored. By training the model using robust training methods, it is possible to enhance the model's resistance to adversarial attacks. Therefore, it is recommended that in future works, robust training methods be combined with the blend GAN training method to determine if a combination of these methods can significantly improve the model's resistance to adversarial attacks. The implementation details and code for the robust training method are available online

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is vital in medical imaging. Recent approaches often rely on datasets from a single hospital, which may lead to issues when applied to datasets from other hospitals due to variations in lesion appearance and clinical protocols. Previous studies typically addressed these dataset disparities by training models from scratch using combined datasets, which is resource-intensive. Instead, adaptive models that continue learning with new data have the potential to improve segmentation when transferred to new datasets. We found, however, that continuing to train an existing model using a new dataset similar to its own dataset atlas results in performance degradation, likely due to overfitting to the new dataset. On the other hand, continuing to train an adaptive model using a new dataset more focused on generic lesion patterns actually leads to improved performance and increased robustness. This research is the first to explore ongoing training methods for segmentation tasks and evaluates their effectiveness in medical image processing. We aim for our study to lay the groundwork for ongoing training to enhance model performance when transferred to new datasets, ultimately contributing to improved automated segmentation in a more data-efficient manner. The code for this study can be accessed at https://github.com/alexandrasveinsson/ms_seg_ongoing_training. As an additional contribution, we also studied the impact of hyperparameters in ongoing training and produced a best-practice guideline. The study was conducted under real-world settings with real data and developed using open-source tools, specifically openminds and openmri-toolbox. Research on contrast properties in visual perception has been extensively conducted across various fields and studies.  Initially, the concept was linked to differences in brightness and/or colors, but it has since been expanded to include contrasts involving other attributes, such as shape and texture.  The primary goal of contrast research is to grasp how the human visual system processes internal and external stimuli, including adaptations to environmental factors like light and overall signal strength.  Theoretical frameworks for contrast have been developed, but the issue is complex and not yet fully understood.  Notably, the term 'bipolar' has not previously been used to describe contrasts, where variations are compared against a uniform baseline; instead, the concept has focused on differences between distinct items.  A newly proposed theory of Bipolar Contrast, however, suggests that contrasts can be viewed as simple bipolar processes, where the baseline is the average of two states.  A simple mathematical model has also been created to simulate how such a contrast system could be perceived by the human vision system and influence behavioral responses.  The new theory provides a unified perspective on various contrast effects and sheds light on the underlying cognitive mechanisms, thus offering a potential foundation for future theoretical developments. We've developed an artificial intelligence framework that identifies dynamic system model faults. By simultaneously generating data from both the correct and incorrect model equations, we create a transfer learning environment. The AI is then challenged to distinguish between states derived from the accurate model and those generated from the inaccurate one. By integrating this approach with transfer learning, we enhance the AI's ability to detect model inaccuracies on datasets obtained from the inaccurate model. Furthermore, we've discovered that letting the AI iterate through both models acts as an economic penalty, limiting the AI's capacity to perfectly mimic noisy data from just the flawed model. This technique has been successfully tested on a nonlinear filter created from a Lorenzian wheel balance system. The results show that our method can effectively identify subtle flaws in highly complex dynamic systems. This breakthrough has significant implications for advanced predictive system frameworks, allowing for more robust predictive systems that can withstand potential model flaws. The development of these techniques may facilitate the creation of predictive models for complex problems like weather and climate modeling, where there are no established correct models. The approach can potentially be adapted for parametric model identification, state estimation, and planning. The general framework is also compatible with deep learning. This research marks the first attempt at using AI to identify and correct model flaws in dynamic systems. The combination of using machine learning algorithms on numerical simulations represents a relatively new area known as simulomics. The results show that machine learning on simulomics data can yield computationally efficient model validation procedures in the absence of extensive modeling expertise. The optimality of our method has yet to be determined. The utility of this research lies in its potential to develop reliable software for increasingly complex systems, a need that has been overlooked in the literature. The framework is suitable for a variety of machine learning algorithms, including those that utilize gradient information and those that do not. The method requires the integration of both the flawed and correct model equations, making it incompatible with situations where there is only one potential model. The approach can be applied to a wide range of systems, including nonlinear, initially unknown, and ordinary differential equation systems. The results reveal that using data from just the correct model is insufficient for detecting model flaws, and that data from both models is necessary. The method works with dynamic system models, but it remains to be seen whether it can be applied to more advanced systems like partial and ordinary differential equations. Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) are a prospectiv dark matter candidate,  and their investigation entails a two-fold analysis of the formation and post-formation examination. Our focus lies solely on the initial PBH formation, which necessitates the use of the linear pressurized two-fluid model (PFHM) for an accurate description. However, coding this model results in a computationally intensive task. In contrast, the pressurized two-fluid analytic calculation for PBH formation (PopSyCLE) presents an efficient yet precise method. Our code offers a fast, straightforward approach, leading to minimal computational time of around 0.005 milliseconds for each calculation. Based on these results, the applications of PopSyCLE are demonstrated through various PBH formation scenarios, encompassing different initial scales and pressure laws. These results are further illustrated in a PBH mass function and compared with other approaches like multimessenger simulations and mechanical instability theories. In addition, the applications of PopHOLE, a companion code that accounts for initial inhomogeneities, are discussed. In particular, the use of PopSyCLE and PopHOLE are combined to explore supermassive PBHs formed by the merger of smaller primordial black holes. In a different scenario, the influence of different nonlinear density laws is also examined, and the associated implications are discussed. Lastly, the predictions of some models based on PopSyCLE and PopHOLE are presented without corresponding references, and the related code is made available at GitHub under the MIT license. In conclusion, the efficient yet precise code PopSyCLE is suited for PBH formation parameters, whereas PopHOLE is designed for PBH abundance. The research involves simulating and analyzing the behavior of a mixture containing flat-sided spheres in a specific arrangement, where the flat sides face each other, using molecular dynamics simulations. The unique structure of this mixture allows for the existence of hexagonal packing, which contributes to the presence of pentagonal holes and irregularly shaped voids in the lattice. The study reveals the presence of two distinct phases: an ordered phase with modulated orientation and a disordered phase, which exhibits threedimensional (3D) disorder with varying particle spacing. The analysis shows that the modulated phase exhibits variations in the spacing between layers, controlled by the angle of the spheres' flat sides, within a specific range of angles. The study also shows that the strength of the interparticle interactions and the shape of the spheres' ends can influence the phases and layer spacing of the modulated phase. The findings provide a framework for understanding and analyzing the behavior of certain soft-matter systems. The estimated range of parameters for stabilizing a modulated phase in the studied system is: hexagonal packing parameter $0.76\le\gamma\le0.95$, polar parameter $0.5\le\beta\le0.9$, and shape parameter $0.5\le\delta\le0.9$. The calculated enthalpy and entropy parameters for the existing phases indicate that the disordered phase should dominate in a range of weak to moderate interactions, which may involve soft materials with dipole or van der Waals forces. The calculated pressure for the existing phases shows that the modulated phase should exhibit high pressure in a range of weak to moderate polar interactions. The study's predictions can guide experimental searches for similar phases in systems composed of hard wedges composed of spheres. The estimated pressure for the existing phases suggests that experimental searches for a modulated phase should focus on systems with polar interactions. The study's predictions for the range of parameters and layer spacing of the modulated phase can guide experimental searches for similar phases in systems involving dipole or van der Waals forces. The study's predictions for the range of parameters and layer spacing of the modulated phase can guide experimental searches for similar phases in systems with various types of interactions. Language model pre-training is followed by downstream task fine-tuning in many contemporary frameworks. However, the conventional fine-tuning technique, which adjusts model parameters based on task data, often suffers from efficiency issues and parameter redundancy. To address these bottlenecks, researchers have introduced various methods of optimizing the fine-tuning process, such as adjusting a small subset of model parameters with low computational requirements or enabling task data to influence the model's token representations directly. Nevertheless, the existing solutions have limitations in either efficiency or effectiveness. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a special token adaptation method for efficient fine-tuning. By introducing a set of special tokens to encode task labels and incorporating them into the model architecture, our method allows the model to take advantage of token adaptation with enhanced efficiency. The proposed method has been evaluated on three natural language processing benchmarks, yielding superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods in terms of both efficiency and effectiveness. Specifically, our method has achieved a significant 68% reduction in fine-tuning computation cost and a 30% reduction in the number of adjusted parameters, with resulting improvements in evaluation metrics such as Matthew's correlation coefficient, F1 score, and EM score of 6%, 6%, and 15% respectively. The method's source code is available for public access at https://github.com/autopyle/pytorch-interact. Our findings have been presented at the ACM Conference of the Association for Computing Machinery Transactions on Algorithms (ACM TRANS ALGO) and the Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (NAACL). The associated publication can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.04.25 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.06025. When working with preferences, context is crucial - the circumstances that shape an individual's likes and dislikes. While experts agree that context matters, the way we utilize this concept in preference learning is still evolving. This study differentiates between non-contextual and contextual preference modeling approaches, particularly in relation to the set addition problem. Non-contextual models, which treat preferences as standalone, absolute evaluations, often converge to consistent models regardless of the problem's setup. In contrast, contextual models, which view preferences as means-end analyses relating options to valuable goals, can take advantage of the set addition problem's structured information and produce more accurate models. By leveraging rich goal-related data, contextual models can reduce hyperparameter uncertainty and outperform non-contextual models across various experimental setups. Although stand-alone performance might not be impressive, contextual models excel particularly when dealing with incomplete or noisy data. Due to the growing need for effective preference learning algorithms, this study makes a substantial contribution by introducing a new method - Contextual Generalized Apportionment (CGA) - and conducting comprehensive comparisons between non-contextual and contextual approaches. CGA is a type of contextual model developed in this study and achieves state-of-the-art results, outperforming existing methods within the context of set addition problems. Moreover, CGA's potential for real-world applications is discussed along with potential extensions of the research. The findings and code are documented to facilitate reproducibility. When preferences are learned without considering context, crucial information is lost, which can lead to suboptimal decision-making. This study emphasizes the importance of context in preference learning and provides a new method, CGA, to extract valuable insights from data, particularly in areas like public policy, economics, and business decision-making. Also included are several novel contextual preference modeling techniques that are not covered in the main conclusions. These contributions involve 1) the introduction of the Contextual Measuring Act (CMA) for defining goal-related qualities and 2) Generalized Contextual Apportionment (GCA) for broadly applicable tasks beyond set addition problems. These novel ideas illustrate the significance of context in preference modeling and influence many areas of research.

Our simulations simulate the evolution of polymer fluids with larger sizes to analyze their glass transition development over extended time periods. By linking specific simulation outcomes to known thermodynamic properties, we establish accurate thermodynamic properties for observation. These simulations provide thermodynamic information about systems at active relaxation times, enabling us to identify liquid instability areas and locate the terminal bag-transition. Furthermore, these calculations allow us to determine the relative entropy rates in two bag-transitions and demonstrate their association with the entropic component of the free energy. Consequently, these relative entropy rates can be utilized to determine the free energy's configurational part. For easier direct comparison with past works, we present our findings in the form of dimensionless ratios. We also determine the relative entropy rates for the terminal bag-transition and express them in terms of the relative entropy rate of the VFT model and the terminal bag-transition's relaxation time. Our study shows that the entropic component of the free energy to the total free energy ratio is always in the range of 68 to 76 percent. These percentages could offer valuable approximations for future experiments trying to extract the free energy's configuration part from observational data. Using the relative entropy rates in two bag-transitions for calibrating the fictive temperature in past works, we observe significant discrepancies. These discrepancies arose mainly from the substantial systematic error in past works and their limited accessible time domain. Consequently, developing techniques to accurately determine the entropic and convective cooling parts under dynamic conditions is essential. We provide practical guidelines for future studies to establish a well-coordinated thermodynamic-dynamic relationship that simulates the glass formation's thermodynamic characteristics through dynamic observations. Moreover, we propose a new relative entropy rate in the past works to enable them to determine the fictive temperature with minimal uncertainty. Our approach to entropy dynamics is versatile and can be applied to various systems to establish a dynamic understanding of their thermodynamic properties. We plan to apply this method in our future studies on the entropy dynamics of soft matter.

In Neural Machine Translation, the focus phenomenon where rare words are translated last has been a common observation. Motivated by this observation, we propose an optimization direction for generating words during translation. We suggest a regularization method, called Look-Ahead Focus (LAF), which encourages the model to prioritize words based on their rarity. Unlike previous studies that only analyzed post-generation statistics, our proposed LAF technique proactively influences generation by incorporating a fine-grained sensitivity of the decoding process to word rarity. Experimental results on both extrinsic and intrinsic evaluation methods demonstrate that applying LAF significantly improves translation quality. Furthermore, we have found that combining LAF with existing techniques that regulate decoding order is both feasible and effective. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that optimizing generation towards a specific outcome can yield enhanced translation quality. The Findings' repository includes supplementary material. Hirose, \textit{et~al.} in \cite{HLMTY21} introduced h-transform, a general method to evaluate arithmetic Asian options by transforming the original stochastic process into an equivalent one with specific characteristics, making it possible to apply known formulae to obtain the option value. This note highlights the necessity of conditions that ensure the existence and uniqueness of the h-transform, and points out errors in the original paper regarding key stochastic processes. Furthermore, the h-transform is shown to be applicable not only to geometric Asian options but also to other types of options within the family of power-reversed geometric Brownians and provides a correct solution to the problem in \textit{cf.} \cite{HLMTY21}. The h-transform is also employed to derive a general pricing formula for knock-in knock-out options with double barriers. Lastly, the h-transform is used to derive a pricing formula for quoted prices, but due to its complexity, the author suggests the use of Monte Carlo simulations in practice. The Monte Carlo simulations are exemplified with numerical results for various parameters and examples. This paper's additional contributions include the derivation of the h-transform for other types of options within the family of power-reversed geometric Brownians, particularly with $\alpha=1/2$, and the derivation of the h-transform for double barriers in \textbf{Appendix~A} and the Monte Carlo simulations in \textbf{Appendix~B}. The h-transform is a versatile tool that can be used not only for option pricing but also for other applications, such as risk analysis and optimization. For instance, the h-transform can be employed to calculate the Boness operator for fair value markup in \textbf{Appendix~C}. \newline The author would like to express his sincere gratitude to Professor Takashi Goto for his continuous support and encouragement, particularly for introducing his relevant works \cite{GTO18} \cite{GTO20} on the h-transform, as well as Professor Hideki Takahashi for his valuable comments and suggestions. Machine-learning applications increasingly demand robust and comprehensible systems. In areas like image recognition, comprehensibility means users should grasp why a specific image corresponds to a particular class. By incorporating visual explanations, users can gain insight into the decision-making process of a model. Unfortunately, interpreting the complex conclusions drawn by deep neural networks remains challenging. Research has identified the source of these complexities in the multiple generalised kernel predictors within these networks. To address this issue, a novel approach, latent visual explanation (LVE) has been introduced. LVE consists of three key components: visual filters with semantic meanings, kernel selection, and kernel weighting. Each filter is assumed to highlight distinct semantic aspects, and the kernel selection mechanism determines which filters are relevant and how many to use. Lastly, kernel weighting assigns importance to each selected filter. When applied to image classification, LVE successfully captures multiple, intricate class-specific patterns, enabling faster convergence and more accurate predictions. Moreover, LVE enables comprehensible image classifications by pinpointing regions that define each unique pattern. The proposed LVE can also be extended to other computer vision tasks such as image discrimination and ranking. Importantly, LVE integrates both localisation and attribution techniques to achieve these tasks. Using a focused attention mechanism as an example, it becomes apparent that LVE facilitates semi-interpretability. Evaluating the skills of these workers presents a significant challenge, particularly when tasks require expert knowledge. In the field of health communication, we've found it difficult to find qualified workers on crowdsourcing platforms, such as Amazon Mechanical Turk. Our study aims to understand the issue by investigating three key aspects: (i) the variability of TurkWorker qualifications, (ii) the effectiveness of filtering methods based on demographic information and task-specific qualifications, and (iii) the existence of fake TurkWorker IDs and how they impact study results. Our findings suggest that while US-based TurkLogic qualifications may align with health-related skills, other demographic qualifications show no consistent correlation with similar tasks. Furthermore, we discovered that workers can create multiple TurkLogic profiles using the same IP address, creating a potential bias in filtering methods. Moreover, we found that hiring pseudo-workers on MTurk can be particularly costly and may lead to biased results. Our study highlights the need for researchers to rigorously validate the qualifications of MTurk workers or adopt alternative filtering strategies. Additionally, we recommend that MTurk developers prevent multi-account registrations and fake pseudo-worker recruitment. Our findings contribute to the development of more ethical crowdsourcing practices and outline a framework for establishing the expertise of MTurk workers. Upcoming high-intensity muon colliders will operate beams with extremely high currents, necessitating extremely low levels of background noise to meet their precision requirements. Nevertheless, these beams will inevitably produce a substantial number of beam splitters, yielding more than 10^9 particles per meter traveled, and, as a result, it will be extremely challenging to lower background noise below the 10^-5 zone without using specialized methods. This problem may be addressed through a range of strategies for reducing background noise to be as small as feasible, with the aim of achieving minimal noise levels. The strategies include enhancing magnetic field quality, using active and reactive methods to manipulate the muon beam, utilizing halo reduction procedures, implementing optical feedback control, utilizing particle identification techniques, and exploiting the characteristics of the coherent radiation spectrum. The analysis indicates that a combination of these methods has the potential to reduce background noise to 10^-5 z, as well as provide guidance on the relative efficiency of each technique, with the aim of achieving an optimal solution. Furthermore, it is anticipated that implementing these strategies at the CLD test facility will yield concrete data to verify that these methods can effectively reduce background noise. The analysis presents specific design modifications required to achieve noise minimization as well as simulated results demonstrating the feasibility of the technique and the relative effectiveness of each strategy in the context of beam design. The strategies are divided into two categories: (1) methods to minimize coherent and incoherent fringe field background; (2) methods to minimize incoherent trident background. Each category is discussed in more detail. The first category includes the use of magnetic field adjustments and various types of feedback control. The second category incorporates muon energy loss manipulation and halo size reduction. Additionally, this paper presents an assessment of particle identification approaches to measure the identification loss of already detected muons and proposed methods to prevent identification loss of these muons. The final section explores long-range strategy options to minimize background noise at future high-energy colliders. Notably, this paper outlines a plan to establish a realistic beam design aimed at achieving optimal noise reduction with minimal emittance damping and halo size. The analysis demonstrates that a realistic beam design can effectively reduce incoherent background noise to 10^-5 and pion background noise to 10^-4 z. Ultimately, it is anticipated that these strategies will contribute to achieving the desired goal of achieving very low background noise at the muon collider. The corresponding noise reduction concepts will be put into practice at the CLD test facility to verify the effectiveness of the strategies.

Empirical software engineering research often draws a large response from industry professionals, as it provides valuable insights into practical issues. A key factor in achieving empirical results is the participation of experienced developers in studies. Prior research has investigated end-users' perception of the severity of relevant software metrics, but developers' opinions have not been tapped into. This paper aims to fill this knowledge gap by examining the severity of test smells as viewed by developers through the lens of the Maintainability Index. Our results reveal a connection between the deployable level of code and the severity of test smells, as well as interesting parallels between the perspectives of end-users and developers. Our findings suggest that developers rate test smells slightly more severely than end-users and that the associations between test smells and the Maintainability Index are less prominent in the developer dataset. Our analysis highlights differences in the potential value of empirical software engineering results for practitioners and researchers. A greater involvement of practical stakeholders is necessary to fully understand the impact of test smells. Our study demonstrates the usefulness of large-scale surveys in uncovering complex empirical software engineering results. A comprehensive replication recipe, including all data and replication artifacts, is available online at https://dx.survey.com/rep223. Our replication recipe replicates our empirical findings in different contexts, thus contributing to the software engineering body of knowledge. Our current research highlights the significance of the scope of the studied samples and the variety of experts involved. A more extensive, diversified sample of developers would help to solidify our empirical results. Such a study could be conducted as part of a PhD research, employing quantitative methods to gather data from a wide range of programming platforms and communities. A practical limitation of our research is the lack of distinct, fundamental types of test smells, which hinders our understanding of their underlying nature. A follow-up study could investigate the frequency of test smell occurrence across different programming paradigms to shed light on their fundamental characteristics. Our research encourages the software engineering community to participate in empirical studies to advance our understanding of various practical issues. A knowledge project on GitHub, akin to the one described in Section \ref{sec:project}, could help to disseminate our empirical results to a large audience of practitioners. Our paper ultimately advocates for increased participation from developers and other stakeholders in empirical software engineering research. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted. Recent advancements in denoising techniques have significantly improved ECG denoising, yet they have significant drawbacks when applied to noisy ECG signals. Our research presents a pioneering approach that uses a tiramisu auto-encoder to filter noisy IBIs. By incorporating statistical data on heart rate and a novel cost function, we have developed an algorithm that accurately estimates IBIs even in highly distorted environments. Extensive testing has shown that our method delivers the lowest error rate compared to existing techniques. Additionally, we have created a cardiovascular disease dataset and conducted a study that compares the efficacy of IBIs estimated by our method with that of competitive denoising techniques. Our results show that the tiramisu algorithm yields the lowest loss value, indicating its superiority in real-world applications. Recent experiments have yielded a highly unstable $^7$H isotope with specific properties. Notably, theoretical calculations have determined its half-life and cross-sections for different reactions. However, these studies conflicted with each other and with established nuclear standards, prompting changes to the literature. In response, we revisit the problem by reconsidering the $^7$H ground state using an effective field theory for few-nucleon systems and expanding the theory to include spin and isospin. We re-examine the ground state as a specific excitation involving three protons and four neutrons, and by applying this analysis, we explain the observed reaction cross-sections and the revised half-life, aligning with updated nuclear data for three and four neutron-hydrogen systems. In the process, we discuss the impact of theoretical calculations on the revision to the nuclear standards in the field of epithermal neutron-capture cross-sections. Furthermore, we use this analysis to interpret the experimental signs of isospin symmetry breaking in the $^7$H isotope. The considered theoretical ground state also serves as a starting point for analyzing rare $^7$H isotope ionization using an electron-proton scattering cross-section, and by extrapolating this analysis, we can potentially relate it to the electron-neutron cross-section in the neutron-hydrogen ($^1$H) system. Moreover, we use this analysis to interpret the experimental Isospin Symmetry Breaking (ISB) parameters in the $^7$H isotope using the known $^7$H neutron transfer reaction, and demonstrate its relevance to neutron properties. In the process of these analyses, we have obtained some relevant fine structure constants including the neutron self-energy, and the ISB parameters in the neutron. These values agree with other existing theoretical calculations except for the ISB parameters which are still under debate and have varying results. In the process of these analyses, we have also identified certain numerical issues with these parameters, and potentially resolved these problems. Furthermore, we proceed to develop more detailed theories for these parameters, and to explore their potential significance in the field of hadronic physics and the study of Isospin Symmetry Breaking (ISB) in hadrons. The inverse problem for the Nirenberg equation on half-spheres leads to a constrained nonlinear eigenvalue problem. We analyze the solutions of this problem by considering a related unitary representation of the orthogonal group. We focus on solving this problem for the z-component of the field, given a fixed total spin s and multiplicity l, to obtain the eigenvalue eigenfunction. Our approach involves analyzing finite blow-ups of the given constraint, using blow-up techniques in conjunction with the mu-invariant notions, traditionally applied in conformal geometry. We discover that the most trivial solution, having the highest degree of irreducibility, is not the only one when l is odd. Non-trivial solutions exist, corresponding to an algebraically decoupled part and an irreducible part, which is supported on the equator. We also demonstrate that these non-trivial solutions can be obtained as blow-ups of the trivial solution. Furthermore, since the constraint has an invariant of degree d for d from 3 to l+1, we obtain a differential identity related to this invariant, which is associated with a non-trivial solution, leading to a new implicit ordinary differential system on the equator, whose integration gives a non-trivial solution of the constrained eigenvalue problem. In our research, we evaluate how the local tracing efforts of private companies are influencing the efficiency of England's COVID-19 contact tracing operation.  We compare the overall efficiency of the tracing system in areas where private companies are actively participating, to the efficiency in areas where they are not.  We have discovered that areas working closely with private companies tend to have a higher tracing efficiency, with a larger proportion of their contacts being successfully identified.  Notably, private company led tracing efforts have prioritized certain groups within society, focusing more on testing and tracing individuals in schools, care homes, and across broader society, as opposed to the approach taken by the NHS test and trace.  We explain the higher efficiency through factors such as the reduced size of the contact list, better coverage among secondary contacts, and an enhanced capability to follow-up with contacts.  Moreover, we reveal that the testing of secondary contacts has been more effective in areas under private company control.  We offer potential justifications for these observations and explore their implications in relation to the existing debate surrounding the role of private companies within test and trace operations in the UK.  Furthermore, we discuss the broader societal consequences of test and trace efficiency, with reduced efficiency potentially resulting in the failure to prevent an increase in infections, hospitalisations, and broader mortality rates.  Using data available up to 16th March 2021, our research provides timely insights relevant to the current period, yet our conclusions may hold significant value even in a potential third COVID-19 wave. Moreover, our insights could be applied in various contact tracing scenarios for infectious diseases.  This research forms part of a larger project titled 'Private Companies in COVID-19 Test and Trace Operations in the UK: Efficiency, Health, and Other-Monetary Outcomes'.  To better facilitate policy-making, we are exploring several related policy questions, the findings of which will be made publicly available once the study is completed. In this paper, we establish key findings related to minimal vertex sets within infinite hypergraphs. A hypergraph is considered minimal if its vertices cannot be partitioned into separate subsets where the subsets are isolated from each other. We show that a hypergraph with a certain type of connected component must contain a unique minimal vertex set comprising just one vertex. Additionally, if the hypergraph's component has infinite size and is a subset of a specific topological space, then it must contain at least one of three possible minimal vertex configurations. We provide an example illustrating that a hypergraph's minimal vertex sets can't be fully described by their cardinality without further assumptions. We prove that hypergraphs meeting certain density criteria have an upper limit on the number of minimal vertex sets within them, and that in such cases, these sets can be categorized based on the size of their smallest monochromatic subset. We describe a formula enabling computation of a hypergraph's topological diameter, defining it as the minimum integer value needed to connect all vertices of the hypergraph through a sequence of combinations. We show that for hypergraphs with a certain type of minimal vertex set having at most two distinct elements, these sets can be fully characterized using the values of the hypergraph's primitive spectra. We discuss a relation between minimal vertex sets and self-dual hypergraphs, and identify necessary and sufficient conditions under which a hypergraph having a certain type of minimal vertex set can be transformed into its self-dual counterpart. We prove that a hypergraph consisting of just three non-monochromatic subsets cannot be minimal, and define a subset relation among all possible types of minimal vertex sets within a hypergraph, depending on the number of distinct elements they contain. The interconnection between thousands of domain-specific terms within extensive knowledge graphs poses significant analysis challenges. This issue arises particularly often when examining vast ontologies within fields like law, medicine, and engineering. Within this context, understanding relationships between related concepts and identifying unanticipated connections is of utmost importance. One such relationship consists of pairs featuring a main concept and one of its subordinate ideas, often depicted as 'is-a' associations in hierarchical frameworks. However, only a minimal fraction of these subordination links can be found in documented knowledge graphs. This study introduces OntoPlot, a innovative visualization tool designed to uncover non-hierarchical connections among large-scale ontologies through clustering-related terms and generating top-level visual representations. We incorporate an innovative technique for detecting implicit associations within datasets, and subsequently assess its applicability for visualizing such findings. We analyze and examine the potential practical uses of this method through a real-world case study involving a German legislation dataset. The research behind OntoPlot provides valuable insights into visual methods for identifying and categorizing associations within vast knowledge graphs. The Soret effect is a temperature phenomenon that shows different components of a homogeneous mixture have varying rates of diffusion due to their unique average molecular energies. Although primarily studied in gas states, our research reveals that the Soret effect also significantly affects the behavior of flexible molecules in dense liquids. Through Computational Molecular Dynamics simulations, we found that the Soret effect is strongly influenced by the internal movements of molecules. Conversely, the arrangement of rigid molecules within the framework of dense liquids shows minimal sensitivity towards temperature variations. Our research thereby highlights the considerable role internal molecular energies play in shaping thermal diffusion phenomena. Besides offering a deeper understanding of internal molecular interactions, our findings also imply that flexible molecules possess additional channels for releasing energy at molecular levels. The global solvability of the Davey-Stewartson II equations is demonstrated for initial data pairs $(u, v)$ in specific $L^2$ subspaces by using a second-kind integral operator $K_{LS}$ associated with the Schrödinger equation. By establishing that $K_{LS}$ is bounded for $|k|$ behavior, this issue is resolved, showcasing an additional application of this operator beyond its standard use in proving local solvability in frequency-space. The findings of the current study are considered robust enough to cover the one-dimensional case of the two-dimensional DSII equation. Interestingly, while the choice of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ is sufficient for one-dimensional studies, it leads to the intriguing possibility of infinitely many connected components for the support of $u$ and $v$. A smallness condition is required to prevent the emergence of singularities due to the interaction between the Schrödinger and Euler Riemann $\mathfrak{R}$ components of $K_{LS}$. The work presented here is an enhancement of the researcher's previous studies on the DSII equations and serves as a preparation for an upcoming study on the DSII equations in three-dimensional space. Furthermore, it provides theoretical support for the recently developed paper by C. Cabralho et al. regarding numerical simulations of the Davey-Stewartson II equations. The approach in the current study, relying on the use of $K_{LS}$ in frequency-space, complements the approach in the aforementioned numerical simulations paper, utilizing a Lagrangian approach in the Lagrangian space of the DSII equations. Moreover, it is proven that the diffusive Euler Riemann $\mathfrak{R}$ component of $K_{LS}$ is well-suited for the creation of decoupling schemes in the Lagrangian space, previously unexplored in the study by C. Cabralho et al. Consequently, it is suggested that this investigation should be part of a future study that will also cover the three-dimensional DSII equations. High-dimensional data cannot be effectively learned by simple, distributed representations unless there is a structural connection limiting the number of parameters. We introduce two proof-of-concept algorithms that focus on learning a linear transformation to create a low-dimensional representation which can accurately reconstruct the original data and perform well in subsequent classification tasks. The first approach, called Manifold, utilizes stochastic gradient descent to find a low-dimensional representation and incorporates an additional term in its objective function to ensure its invertibility. However, when working with real-world datasets, not all Invertible CCA representations are beneficial. To address this, we present MonoDA, which selects the most useful representation from a set of investigated possibilities. Our analysis, performed using MRI images, demonstrates that these representations lead to significant improvements in classification accuracy and are understandable, specifically in the context of multiple-class melanoma classification. We compare our method with established baseline algorithms, such as AdaGMM and CGEN. Our findings confirm that they fail to produce useful representations for subsequent tasks, whereas Manifold is able to learn an invertible representation but sometimes results in a higher classification error in some tasks. To the contrary, MonoDA is able to find the most suitable representation from a set of investigated possibilities, thereby achieving better performance than manifold in most of the classification tasks. We showcase the uniqueness of MonoDA's chosen representations through visualizations of their eigenvalues. MonoDA significantly outperforms existing methods, thereby setting a new standard in demonstrable meta-learning with a focus on low-dimensional linear representations.
