When it comes to decreasing the computational burden of deep learning models, including machine translation, quantization and distillation are frequently used methods to lower model size without sacrificing performance. In a study examining the stability of these techniques with training data size, findings reveal that while they each exhibit unique trends with increasing data availability, distillation shows notable improvements with larger datasets, whereas the effectiveness of quantization appears more heavily dependent on the characteristics of the training dataset used. Furthermore, distillation shows greater consistency in its performance compared to quantization. We also investigate the potential to combine these techniques and discover that, in certain situations, sequentially applying distillation followed by quantization results in superior outcomes compared to utilizing quantization alone. Ultimately, this research highlights the importance of selecting the most effective approach to developing efficient low-resource MT models. The source code for this study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/mteodoro/Low-Resource-MT-Lightweight.

The study suggests that distillation could be an effective method for developing lightweight low-resource MT models, potentially surpassing quantization in this context.
When utilizing quantization, it may be beneficial to train the model using a larger dataset to ensure more reliable results.
To optimize the performance of lightweight low-resource MT models, a controlled multistage approach combining distillation and quantization could yield superior outcomes.

The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms in identifying specific regions within medical images is heavily dependent on the quantity and quality of the training data available. In low-resource settings, accessing large datasets of labeled images can be extremely challenging, hindering the implementation of deep learning-based segmentation techniques in real-world clinical settings. In our research, the impact of varying data augmentation techniques on the accuracy of pneumonia segmentation in chest X-ray images was investigated. Additionally, the study examined the trade-off between image quality and accuracy by employing a composite metric. Ultimately, the results showed that utilizing a combination of two data augmentation techniques - image translational enhancement and image brightening - along with a reduced number of labeled images (25% of the total training dataset), was sufficient to match the accuracy of models trained with larger numbers of labeled images. Specifically, the results indicated that using 25% of the total training dataset and combined image augmentation yielded an average mosaic center prediction accuracy of 0.7922, whereas without augmentation but with 25% of the total training dataset, the accuracy was 0.7666. When utilizing larger datasets without any augmentation, the accuracy was 0.8125. These findings suggest that deep learning-based segmentation algorithms can effectively identify specific regions within medical images even with limited data, provided that suitable image augmentation techniques are employed. Consequently, these algorithms have the potential to efficiently address shortages in labeled data commonly encountered in low-resource environments. The research further highlights the importance of accurate segmentation, as evaluated by the mean intersection-over-union score, in reducing prediction errors in pneumonia diagnosis from chest X-ray images. In particular, our results indicate that a threshold of ${\text{I}O}_{U}^{m}_{l}>0.70$ effectively minimizes false positives in pneumonia detection. Ultimately, the research showcases the practical utility of these algorithms in real-world clinical settings. Specifically, our results demonstrate that these algorithms can be used to decrease false positives in pneumonia detection while also decreasing the time required for model retraining following introduction of new imaging modalities in clinical settings. In particular, our results indicate that desegregation of pixels via data augmentation techniques reduces the time required for model retraining from 30 minutes to 2 minutes. Ultimately, the research emphasizes the practical utility of segmentation algorithms in real-world clinical settings. In particular, our results indicate that these algorithms can be used to decrease false positives in pneumonia detection and decrease the time required for model retraining following introduction of new imaging modalities in clinical settings. Image description generation, a crucial aspect of vision-language research, involves generating detailed descriptions of images based on a specific perspective. Current models can produce generic descriptions but struggle with personalized description tasks, such as creating descriptions tailored to different perspectives. Our research introduces a Controllable Image Description Model (CIDM) that allows users to input custom prompts and produces descriptions tailored to those prompts. Unlike previous models, CIDM can generate descriptions in response to prompts without requiring pre-training on descriptive datasets and is instead fine-tuned on image-caption datasets with prompt-emulating regularization. Our experiments show that CIDM successfully incorporates the prompt's intention into the description while maintaining its inherent knowledge, even when the prompt is ambiguous. Furthermore, CIDM can produce descriptions with altered attributes by fine-tuning the model with attribute labels, enabling it to generate descriptions according to both prompts and attributes. By leveraging prompts instead of pre-defined attributes, CIDM offers greater flexibility and control over the description generation process. Our findings indicate that CIDM outperforms existing Controllable Image Generation models, such as Controllable Image Generation via Caption Embeddings (CIGLE), both qualitatively and quantitatively. Ultimately, IDM demonstrates its potential as a versatile image description model capable of addressing an array of vision-language challenges. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI-SAILLAB-CU/Controllable-Image-Description-Model. As an extension of our work, we also develop a general-purpose image description model, called Image Description Generation via Unsupervised Pre-training (IDGUP), which is capable of generating descriptions in various styles and can be applied to different image description tasks. IDGUP is available at https://github.com/AI-SAILLAB-CU/Image-Description-Generation-via-Unsupervised-Pre-training. Our contributions are validated through thorough experimental studies. Ultimately, IDGUP and its applications reveal the significant progress made possible by leveraging the two-stream vision-language autoencoder architecture and two-stage decoding process in vision-language research. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI-SAILLAB-CU/Controllable-Image-Description-Model. The distinction between harm and burden highlights the importance of considering how actions affect individuals differently. This paper explores the concept of harm in the context of actions and their effects on agents. It identifies robust harm, which is a causal phenomenon, and outlines its characteristics. Key principles include the principles of causality, comparability, and alterability. To illustrate these principles, the authors describe a scenario involving climate change and carbon emissions. They also discuss additional concepts such as the principle of proportionality and the concept of harm alterability. These principles inform harm mitigation, the evaluation of policies, and the distribution of resources. The authors address objections to their approach and consider implications for philosophical debates. They also expand on the concept of overdetermination, making the case for a more inclusive understanding of causality that applies broadly to real-world scenarios. This causal account of harm aims to inform ethical discussions and harmonize them with empirical realities. It also seeks to integrate this notion into broader philosophical debates. Overall, the methodological framework presented aims to generate actionable ethics. To demonstrate this, the authors describe coherent-moralism, a moral theory grounded in their analysis of harm, to address climate change. Coherent-moralism prioritizes harm mitigation through a multi-step process, beginning with the most significant causes of harm. Each step applies the principle of proportionality, aiming to find the least expensive way to reduce harm. From an economic perspective, the strategy involves maximizing the global welfare potential of carbon emissions, aiming to achieve the largest welfare reduction while complying with the proportionality principle. Through this approach, the authors describe a viable path for reducing emissions and addressing climate change. They acknowledge challenges remain as countries fail to cooperate, and there are ethical debates and limitations to their theory. Nonetheless, the authors believe their framework provides a practical roadmap for ethical guidance in the real world. It is essential to consider the complex nature of harm in international relations and global issues like climate change. This understanding of harm as a causal concept aims to foster a more thoughtful and effective approach to ethics. By applying the principle of comparability without empathy, we can reduce unnecessary suffering and improve the world. This ethical perspective on harm aims to inspire ethical insights and guidance. The key aspect of dynamic interface modeling is accurately capturing the behavior of boundaries that shift over time.  Building upon the foundational work of Coleman and Gurtin in their study of heat flow through a solid with a moving boundary, this research extends their methodology to a broad class of thermodynamic systems, characterized by non-trivial and time-evolving interfaces with spatially constant heat flux.  Despite the initial boundary conditions being non-adiabatic and non-isothermal, the predicted interface behavior remains consistent with classical heat conduction theory under isothermal boundary conditions.  Furthermore, the team has developed a representation theorem for heat flux with significant implications for the theory of evolving surfaces: the total interface energy is unreserved, meaning it can be allocated freely, and interfaces equipped with energy transport can be extended through a transport theorem.  Various examples of evolving surfaces are presented in two-dimensional simulations to illustrate the properties of the model.  Moreover, the model supports the development of a new theory for growing crystals with moving boundaries: here, the model is extended to coupled mass and heat transport on a surface with physically significant results.  Accurate numerical methods are designed to simulate both the Coleman-Gurtin model and the growing crystal model, and are applied in a range of virtual experiments.  The software and related data for these examples are available online through the GitHub repository 'cg-gbc'.  This research has the potential to provide a foundation for a wide-ranging program of simulations in dynamic interface models.  A related movie is accessible at youtube.com/watch?v=u3G6rDZEE0k.  Research is currently being conducted to expand the methodology in this thesis in two directions: developing a new theory of growing crystals with kink boundaries and investigating the potential of these models in real-world applications.  A related software package for the second application is available at github.com/Frank-Voyles/liquid-demoulating-surfactant-system to illustrate this second direction. Precise forecasting of energy consumption is essential to manage low voltage electricity networks effectively, particularly in anticipating peak demand during periods of high usage. To tackle these challenges, studies have previously investigated short-term and long-term forecasting techniques, yet their complexity often hinders their practical application. To address these issues, this research introduces a two-stage performance enhancement method that builds upon existing forecasting methods to improve accuracy and robustness. To model uncertainty in forecasting, a stochastic prediction approach is applied, combining outcomes from the upgraded forecasting systems. We evaluate our approach by analyzing its capabilities in predicting both daily peak and average usage values. The results demonstrate that the proposed method offers high level of performance, with predicted peak values accurate to ±2.5% 75% of the time, and predicted average values accurate to ±1.5% 85% of the time. Furthermore, the integration of the stochastic prediction model enables the reduction of demand forecasting errors by 43%. We validate our approach through experiments using a publicly available dataset from the UMIAG over the period of 2012-2022. We also make my code available to the public via a GitHub repository. Our methodology has been successfully applied in real-world settings, exemplified by a case study of a British low voltage electricity network. The results reveal a reduction in demand costs of approximately £310 per year and an increase in the VRS efficiency score of approximately 0.003, indicating improved performance. Overall, the proposed methodology enhances the precision, robustness, and usability of forecasting tools, particularly in predicting both daily peak and average usage values. Furthermore, the integration of the stochastic prediction model enables the reduction of demand forecasting errors and achieves more accurate and robust results. The success of this approach has real-world implications, exemplified by its application in improving the performance of a British low voltage electricity network. The result of this research and its codes are now freely accessible to the public, enabling other researchers to reproduce and expand on this work. The outcome of this research and its impact on the improvement of demand forecasting methods will contribute to the advancement of future studies. However, the challenge lies in striking a balance between incorporating domain expertise and external knowledge without overwhelming the model. This paper aims to develop a strategic approach for integrating domain knowledge in ML, categorizing domain knowledge into three distinct types - domain specifications, domain descriptions, and domain inferences - based on their relevance to the problem at hand. We will illustrate this framework with two exemplary scenarios, namely, 1) when domain knowledge is insufficient or incomplete, and 2) when existing domain knowledge needs to be expanded upon. This foundation will enable the construction of various algorithms for integrating domain knowledge in ML, which will be discussed in depth. We will also examine potential challenges and discuss future research directions regarding knowledge integration in ML. This work has the potential to significantly contribute to the development of ML algorithms capable of harnessing domain knowledge, ultimately yielding more robust and dependable models. Creating a COVID-19 diagnosis tool based on CT scan analysis involves two key steps: identifying and segmenting lung lesion areas. Due to limited resources and annotation time, the typical approach uses strongly supervised learning. Nevertheless, this method is hindered by biased model performance, largely due to the inherent issues of lesion non-specificity on CT scans. To overcome these challenges, we developed a new framework for unbiased lesion localization and segmentation. This framework exploits the utilization of CT scans with masks applied to Lungs ($M_L$) and masks with COVID lesions mixed ($M_C$) through a dual-stage weakly supervised approach. Initially, we trained a model to identify COVID areas using combined models $M_L$ and $M_C$. Next, we trained another model to generate lesion masks in COVID areas. To promote generalization, we introduced a lesion-specific cross entropy loss and an adversarial regularizer to the model that generates masks. This new loss function pairs with an adversarial network to magnify the distinction between masks applied to Lungs ($M_L$) and those with COVID lesions mboxes ($M_C$) that the model needs to distinguish. This method enhances lesion localization and segmentation to outperform existing approaches on the COVID19-LLC benchmark by 1.9% and 1.3% respectively. Additionally, we demonstrate that our method leads to better unbiased performance when generating CT scan masks in Lungs ($M_L$) from existing models. This method lets us render COVID-free CT scans that are free from artificial markers and also allows us to identify lesions in Lungs ($M_L$) and segment them accurately with the best AUC on the COVID19-LLC benchmark at 87.6%. The code for this paper is found at https://github.com/indigo95/covid19-unbiased-localization-segmentation. The COVID19-LLC benchmark can be found at https://github.com/zzhshd/COVID19-LLC. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain complications like spinal deformities or artificial vertebras (e.g. in tumor cases) can hinder fully automatic approaches. To address these challenges, this paper presents an enhanced, multi-stage framework that surpasses existing automated identification methods. By integrating the statistical properties of spinal curvature and external anatomical information, the proposed technique outperforms the state-of-the-art vertebra localization and identification results, achieving a high degree of precision (98% and 95.6% for L1-S1, respectively). The presented approach distills complex vertebra localization and identification into two manageable sub-tasks: spine rectification and vertebrae identification, leveraging respective specialized techniques. The spine rectification technique, involving vertebrae approximation and corresponding L1-S1 labels, provides a unified representation for identification. Conversely, by exploiting external anatomical constraints and prior knowledge, the vertebrae identification task is reduced to a manageable Min-Max problem. To balance the constraints, an efficient and robust optimization strategy is introduced. The approach is supported by extensive experiments, showcasing its effectiveness in handling spinal deformities and artificial vertebras. We propose a new variational approach to the principle of dimensionality reduction in quantum physics, effectively capturing the essential properties of complex quantum systems with a simplified model. By restricting the underlying Hilbert space of quantum operators to a lower-dimensional subspace defined by a convex, smooth manifold, and adhering to a constrained variational scheme, we reframe the lost information in a meaningful direction within the manifold's tangent space. We exemplify our approach with the loss of information in going from a one-dimensional to a two-dimensional quantum system. Our method is well-suited for use with diverse quantum parameterizations, such as those based on matrix invariants. We apply it to the case of two-dimensional elliptic models for two qubits and one dimensional square wells with a xenon atom, and demonstrate its capacity for efficient reduction of large-scale quantum systems. Additionally, in the interest of practical applicability, we simplify our original constraint relaxation, yielding a symmetric geometric arrangement that is complementary to certain established methods of dimensionality reduction. Our variational method offers stand-alone dimensionality reduction in quantum physics without reliance on any specific model or efficient entanglement theory. Our results align with the outcomes of other established methods, such as the coplanar angle parameterization, but differ for certain distributions of quantum states. Our new approach has potential for use in the machine learning of quantum wavefunctions. We have released Python-based source code (github.com/johnccopeland/cpt3d/tree/main/research/3d) enabling independent application of this method. Please see Ref. for further discussion. To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, providers seek ways to enhance their current installations. By enabling the strategic placement of access points, or routers, within a network, providers can improve its capacity. Since certain locations offer better signal strength than others, precisely placing these access points is crucial. A new technology, IEEE 802.11k, allows networks to optimize their performance by channel information. In the event that an access point does not have a suitable partner, the process is reversed, and the most likely location of the client is calculated using IEEE 802.11v's Spatial Partitioning standard. A performance test then selects the most appropriate access point or extender based on these calculations and channel load.
